choices: Shell form runs a shell as PID 1, and SIGTERM never reaches your Node process
`npm start` needs a `--production` flag inside containers to handle signals
Docker always waits the full ten-second grace period before stopping any container
The image has no `EXPOSE` line, so Docker cannot tell when the port has closed
questions.why: Shell form wraps the command in `/bin/sh -c`, so the shell (and then npm) receives SIGTERM and does not pass it on; after the grace period Docker sends SIGKILL. Use exec form, `CMD ["node", "server.js"]`, and handle SIGTERM to close the server. `EXPOSE` is documentation only.
questions.asked: Slow, ungraceful shutdowns drop in-flight requests on every deploy; knowing exec form and PID 1 is a strong signal.

questions.q: Your Node process runs as PID 1 in a container with no signal handlers. What happens when it receives SIGTERM?
choices: It exits at once, as any process does for the default SIGTERM action
It ignores it, because the kernel skips default actions for PID 1
It restarts itself, because PID 1 is supervised by the Docker daemon
It forwards it to its child processes and waits for them to finish
questions.why: The kernel does not apply default signal actions to PID 1, so a process without a SIGTERM handler keeps running until SIGKILL. Add a `process.on('SIGTERM', ...)` handler that drains the server, or run a tiny init such as `docker run --init` or tini.
questions.asked: A deeper follow-up to exec form; people who have debugged a stuck container know it.

questions.q: What does `EXPOSE 3000` in a Dockerfile actually do?
choices: Publishes port 3000 on the host so the app is reachable from outside
Opens port 3000 in the container's firewall, which is closed by default
Documents the port; you still publish it with `-p` or compose `ports`
Makes the app listen on port 3000 instead of its configured port
questions.why: `EXPOSE` is metadata used by tools and by `-P`; it neither publishes a port nor configures the app. `docker run -p 8080:3000` maps host port 8080 to container port 3000, and the app must listen on 3000 on `0.0.0.0`.
questions.asked: A quick check for people who have only copied Dockerfiles.

questions.q: Your API works with `npm run dev` but inside the container `curl localhost:3000` from the host gets 'connection reset'. The port is published. What is the likely cause?
choices: The app listens on `127.0.0.1`, which inside a container is unreachable from outside
Containers cannot use port 3000, because Docker reserves it for its own engine API
The host firewall blocks every published port until Docker restarts
`curl` needs `--http2` to talk to a process running inside a container
questions.why: Inside the container, loopback is the container's own, so a server bound to `127.0.0.1` refuses traffic arriving on the container's network interface. Bind to `0.0.0.0` (or `::`) in containers.
questions.asked: One of the most common 'works locally, not in Docker' problems; the answer shows you understand container networking.

questions.q: Why is this a bad way to give the build access to a private npm registry?
questions.code:
ARG NPM_TOKEN
RUN echo "//registry.npmjs.org/:_authToken=$NPM_TOKEN" > .npmrc && npm ci
choices: `ARG` values are cleared before `RUN`, so the token is always empty
The token ends up in the image metadata and layers anyone can inspect
npm ignores any `.npmrc` file that is created during a Docker build for security
Build arguments can only hold values shorter than 64 characters
questions.why: Build args used in a `RUN` are recorded in the image history, and the `.npmrc` stays in that layer even if a later step deletes it. BuildKit secret mounts (`RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmrc ...`) expose the file only during that step and never write it to a layer.
questions.asked: Leaked registry tokens in public images are common; the secret-mount answer is what reviewers want.

questions.q: A Dockerfile runs `RUN rm -rf /app/tmp` to delete a 500 MB folder copied in an earlier step. Why does the image not get smaller?
choices: `rm` inside `RUN` only marks files as deleted until the container first starts
Docker compresses deleted files rather than removing them from the image
Deleted files are kept until you run `docker system prune` on the host
Layers are additive: the earlier layer still holds the folder
questions.why: Each instruction adds a layer, and a later deletion only hides the files in the final filesystem view while the earlier layer still ships them. Avoid copying them in (`.dockerignore`), clean up in the same `RUN` that created them, or use a multi-stage build.
questions.asked: Tests whether you understand layers rather than treating a Dockerfile as a shell script.

questions.q: What belongs in `.dockerignore` for a Node app?
choices: `package-lock.json`, because the build should always resolve fresh versions
`Dockerfile`, because Docker cannot copy the file it is currently building
`src/`, because the build stage reads sources from the Git remote instead
`node_modules`, `.git` and `.env`, so they never enter the build context
questions.why: The build context is sent to the builder, so excluding host `node_modules` (wrong platform binaries), `.git` (large, and busts caching) and `.env` (secrets) makes builds faster, smaller and safer. The lockfile must be included for `npm ci`.
questions.asked: A quick practical check; the strong answer says why each entry matters.

questions.q: In Docker Compose, `api` has `depends_on: [db]`. The API still crashes on start because Postgres is not ready. Why?
choices: `depends_on` only affects the order of `docker compose down`, not startup
Plain `depends_on` waits for the container to start, not for Postgres to be ready
Compose starts services in alphabetical order, so `api` is always first
`depends_on` only works when both services are built from the same Dockerfile and context
questions.why: Short-form `depends_on` orders container starts but does not wait for readiness. Give `db` a healthcheck (for example `pg_isready`) and use `depends_on: db: condition: service_healthy`, and still have the app retry its first connection.
questions.asked: Every compose setup hits this; the healthcheck condition plus app-side retries is the full answer.

questions.q: In your compose file, the database maps `"5433:5432"`. Which address should the `api` service use?
choices: `localhost:5433`
`localhost:5432`
questions.why: Services reach each other by service name on the compose network, using the container's port. The `5433` mapping only matters from the host, for example for your SQL client. `localhost` inside `api` is the api container itself.
questions.asked: A small puzzle that shows whether you understand host versus container networking.

questions.q: Your local Postgres data vanished after `docker compose down -v`. What did `-v` do?
choices: It removed the named volumes declared by the compose file
It ran `down` verbosely and printed each removed container
It reset the volumes to the state saved in the image
It deleted only anonymous volumes; named ones are always kept
questions.why: `down` removes containers and networks; `-v` also removes named volumes declared in the file and anonymous volumes, which is where the database lived. Plain `down` would have kept the data.
questions.asked: Everyone does it once; knowing volume lifecycles is the point.

questions.q: In dev you bind-mount the project into the container. The app fails with an 'invalid ELF header' error from a native module. What is wrong?
choices: Bind mounts are read-only, so npm cannot compile native modules
The Node version in the image is too new for native modules
The host's `node_modules` was mounted over the container's platform build
Native modules must be installed with `npm ci --native` when running inside containers
questions.why: Mounting the whole project also mounts the host's `node_modules`, built for macOS or Windows, over the Linux one. Add an anonymous volume for `/app/node_modules` so the container keeps its own, or install inside the container only.
questions.asked: A classic local-dev puzzle; the fix shows you understand mount precedence.

questions.q: You build an image on an Apple Silicon Mac and run it on an x86 server. It fails with `exec format error`. Why?
choices: The server's Docker version is too old for images built on macOS
The image was built for arm64, and the server needs linux/amd64
The entrypoint script has Windows line endings from the Mac
macOS builds images for the Darwin kernel, which Linux cannot run
questions.why: Images are per CPU architecture, and an M-series Mac builds `linux/arm64` by default. Build with `--platform linux/amd64` or produce a multi-arch image with buildx; better still, build in CI on the target architecture.
questions.asked: Very common since Apple Silicon; the strong answer mentions building in CI.

questions.q: You switch the base image from `node:24-slim` to `node:24-alpine` and a dependency with native bindings now fails to load. What is the likely reason?
choices: Alpine removes Node's module loader to save space
Alpine images run Node with ES modules disabled by default, so native imports fail
Alpine uses musl libc, and the prebuilt binary targets glibc
Alpine forbids binaries larger than 5 MB in any image layer
questions.why: Alpine is built on musl rather than glibc, so native binaries compiled for glibc may not load, and packages need musl-specific builds or a compile toolchain. Slim Debian images avoid the issue at a modest size cost.
questions.asked: Tests whether 'smaller image' comes with an understanding of the trade-off.

questions.q: Why run the app as a non-root user inside the container (for example `USER node`)?
choices: Root inside a container cannot open ports, so the app would fail to start
Non-root containers start faster, because root runs extra security checks
Docker Hub rejects images whose final user is root
It limits the damage if the app is compromised or escapes the container
questions.why: Root in a container is root in the kernel's eyes unless user namespaces are configured, so a container escape or a writable host mount becomes far more dangerous. Official Node images ship a `node` user and .NET 8+ images an `app` user.
questions.asked: Baseline container hygiene; interviewers expect it in any production Dockerfile.

questions.q: You move an ASP.NET Core app from a .NET 6 image to `mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:9.0`. Health checks now fail on port 80. Why?
choices: ASP.NET Core 9 no longer supports plain HTTP inside containers
.NET 8+ images listen on port 8080 by default, not 80
The aspnet image blocks ports below 1024 at the firewall level
.NET 9 requires the port to be set in `appsettings.json` only
questions.why: Since .NET 8 the official images set `ASPNETCORE_HTTP_PORTS=8080` so the app can run as the non-root `app` user, which cannot bind below 1024. Update the port mapping and probes, or set the variable explicitly.
questions.asked: A real upgrade gotcha that shows you read release notes.

questions.q: What does this `RUN` line gain over a plain `RUN npm ci`?
choices: Downloaded packages persist between builds without being stored in the image
`node_modules` is cached inside the image so that later `COPY` steps run faster
The layer is shared across every image on the machine to save disk
npm runs offline, so the build works without network access
questions.why: A BuildKit cache mount keeps npm's download cache on the builder between builds, but it is not part of any image layer. It speeds up rebuilds when the lockfile changes; it does not make the build work offline on a cold cache.
questions.asked: A modern Dockerfile optimisation; knowing it is not in the image is the key point.

questions.q: You deploy to Kubernetes. Does the Dockerfile's `HEALTHCHECK` instruction decide when the pod is restarted?
choices: Yes, the kubelet runs it and restarts the container on failure
Yes, but only when no liveness probe is declared in the manifest
No, it is only used when the image is run on Docker Swarm
No, Kubernetes ignores it and uses the probes defined in the manifest
questions.why: Kubernetes does not use Docker's `HEALTHCHECK`; liveness, readiness and startup probes in the pod spec control restarts and traffic. The instruction still helps with `docker run` and Compose's `service_healthy` condition.
questions.asked: Clarifies where health checking lives on each platform, a frequent source of confusion.

questions.q: Where should a containerised web app write its logs?
choices: To a log file inside the container, rotated by the app
To a file on a mounted volume so the logs survive restarts
To stdout and stderr, for the platform to collect
Directly to the log vendor's API from every request handler
questions.why: Container runtimes capture stdout and stderr, which `docker logs`, Kubernetes and every log shipper read. Files inside the container vanish with it and fill its disk; shipping from each handler couples request latency to the vendor.
questions.asked: Part of the twelve-factor mindset; interviewers check you do not reinvent log files.

questions.q: Your production image is distroless and `docker exec -it app sh` fails. How do you inspect the running container?
choices: Rebuild the image with bash added back in, then redeploy it to investigate the problem
Attach a debug container that shares its namespaces, such as `kubectl debug`
Use `docker exec -it app node` to open a shell through Node instead
Distroless containers cannot be inspected at runtime by design
questions.why: Distroless images have no shell by design. An ephemeral debug container (Kubernetes `kubectl debug`, or `docker run --pid=container:app --network=container:app` with a tools image) shares the process and network namespaces so you can inspect without changing the image.
questions.asked: Hardened images are becoming the default; knowing how to debug them avoids 'let us just add a shell back'.

questions.q: In GitHub Actions, Docker builds rebuild every layer on every run. What restores layer caching?
choices: Building with `--no-cache` so Docker stores each layer
Running `docker system prune` before each build
Setting `DOCKER_BUILDKIT=0` to use the classic builder
Using buildx with a cache backend such as `type=gha`
questions.why: Hosted runners start empty, so the local layer cache is gone. `docker/build-push-action` with `cache-from`/`cache-to` pointing at the Actions cache or a registry exports and reuses layers across runs. `--no-cache` and pruning do the opposite.
questions.asked: Connects Docker layer knowledge to CI speed.

questions.q: Which statement about image vulnerability scanning (for example Trivy) in CI is accurate?
choices: It finds known CVEs in OS packages and libraries in the image
It proves the image contains no exploitable vulnerabilities
It only scans your own source code, not the base image
It must run inside the production cluster to be accurate
questions.why: Scanners compare installed package versions in the image with vulnerability databases. They find known issues only, and the base image is usually the largest source of findings, which is why teams update bases regularly and prefer slim or distroless ones.
questions.asked: Supply-chain hygiene; the strong answer mentions triage and base image updates.

questions.q: What is the core idea of trunk-based development with short-lived branches?
choices: Every developer commits straight to main with no review at all
Branches live for a day or two and merge to main behind flags if unfinished
Each release gets a long-lived branch that features are merged into
Main is frozen during releases, and new work continues on a separate develop branch
questions.why: Integrating small changes into main continuously keeps merge conflicts small and main releasable; unfinished features ship dark behind flags. Review still happens on the short-lived PRs. Long-lived release and develop branches are GitFlow's model.
questions.asked: Asked to see whether you understand why long-lived branches hurt, not just which model your last team used.

questions.q: When does a release-branch model (cut `release/2.4`, stabilise, ship) make more sense than deploying main continuously?
choices: When the team has fewer than five developers
When the product is a web app deployed several times a day
When you ship versioned releases and must patch older versions
When tests are fast and the pipeline is fully automated
questions.why: Mobile apps, installed software and libraries ship discrete versions and must hotfix 2.4 while 2.5 is in progress, so a branch per release is useful. A continuously deployed web app has one version in production and gains little from it.
questions.asked: Tests whether you pick a branching model from constraints rather than habit.

questions.q: Production runs `release/3.1`. You fix a critical bug. How do you make sure the fix is not lost in the next release?
choices: Fix it on main, merge main into the release branch, and deploy
Fix it on the release branch only, since main will be rewritten anyway
Fix it in production directly, then commit the same change later
Fix it on one branch and cherry-pick it to the other, or merge back
questions.why: Whether you fix on main and cherry-pick to the release branch, or fix on the release branch and merge back, the fix must land on both, or the next release regresses. Merging all of main into a release branch drags in unreleased features.
questions.asked: Regressions from forgotten hotfixes are a real failure mode; interviewers want the 'land it in both places' habit.

questions.q: Which version sorts first under semantic versioning?
choices: They are all equal, since only major.minor.patch counts
questions.why: A pre-release suffix makes a version lower than the plain release, so `2.0.0-rc.1` < `2.0.0`. Build metadata after `+` is ignored for precedence, so `2.0.0+build.5` equals `2.0.0`.
questions.asked: Relevant to publishing packages and release candidates; build metadata is the trap.

questions.q: What is a canary release?
choices: Deploying to a full staging copy of production that only receives synthetic traffic from load tests
Shipping the new version to a small share of real traffic and widening it if metrics hold
Running old and new versions side by side and switching all traffic at once
Releasing only to internal staff through a separate hostname
questions.why: A canary exposes the new version to, say, 5% of production traffic, compares error rates and latency with the baseline, then widens or rolls back. Switching all traffic at once is blue/green, and staff-only access is dogfooding.
questions.asked: Standard deployment vocabulary; the strong answer names the metrics that gate promotion.

questions.q: A canary at 5% shows the same error rate as the baseline, but p99 latency doubled. What should an automated rollout do?
choices: Promote it, since only the error rate matters for correctness
Promote it, as long as the median latency is unchanged
Hold or roll back, because latency is a gating metric too
Restart the canary pods, then promote once p99 recovers
questions.why: Canary analysis should gate on the signals users feel, including tail latency, not just errors. A doubled p99 often precedes errors under full load, and restarting hides the regression rather than explaining it.
questions.asked: Tests whether you understand that 'no errors' is not the same as 'healthy'.

questions.q: A deploy broke checkout. The fix is a one-line change you are confident in. Roll back or roll forward?
choices: Roll forward always, because rollbacks lose data
Roll back first if it is safe and fast, then ship the fix calmly
Roll back only after the postmortem has confirmed the root cause
Roll forward, but skip CI so the fix lands sooner
questions.why: Restoring service is the priority, and a tested rollback is usually faster and less risky than a rushed fix. Rolling forward is right when rollback is unsafe, for example after an irreversible migration, and it still goes through CI.
questions.asked: A judgement question; skipping CI under pressure is the answer interviewers are hoping you avoid.

questions.q: Why should the same built artifact be promoted from staging to production rather than rebuilt for production?
choices: Rebuilding takes longer, which delays the release by a few minutes
Rebuilding can produce different bits than the ones you tested
Production registries only accept images pushed from staging
Staging artifacts contain debug symbols that production needs
questions.why: A rebuild may pull different dependency or base-image versions and produce something that was never tested. Build once, tag it immutably, and promote that exact artifact with environment-specific configuration injected at deploy time.
questions.asked: Core CD principle; ties into image digests and configuration outside the build.

questions.q: A workflow should build and publish a release whenever a version tag is pushed. Which trigger fits?
choices: `on: release: types: [deleted]`
`on: push: branches: ['v*']`
`on: schedule` with a daily cron
`on: push: tags: ['v*']`
questions.why: Tag filters under `push` run the workflow when a matching tag is pushed, and `github.ref_name` then holds the version. A `branches` filter matches branch names, not tags.
questions.asked: Practical release automation; follows naturally from tagging questions.

questions.q: What is the main hidden cost of feature flags, and how do teams control it?
choices: They slow every request, so flags are evaluated only at startup
They require a vendor, so teams build their own flag service
Stale flags pile up as dead branches; give each an owner and removal date
They break caching, so flagged pages must disable HTTP caching
questions.why: Every flag doubles a code path to test, and forgotten flags become permanent complexity or surprise behaviour when flipped years later. Short-lived release flags need an owner, an expiry and a ticket to remove them; long-lived ops flags are documented as such.
questions.asked: Follows 'what is a feature flag'; knowing the cost is the mid-level answer.

questions.q: You roll a feature out to 10% of users with a flag. How should the flag decide which users are in the 10%?
choices: `Math.random() < 0.1` on each request
A stable hash of the user id, bucketed into 100 slots
The first 10% of users to log in each day, tracked in a counter
Users whose id ends in 0, checked in the database
questions.why: Hashing the user id (with the flag key as salt) gives each user a stable bucket, so they see the same variant on every request and widening to 20% keeps the original 10% in. Per-request randomness makes the UI flip between versions.
questions.asked: Tests understanding of sticky assignment, which matters for both UX and experiment validity.

questions.q: What is a kill switch in the context of feature flags?
choices: A flag that shuts down the entire application during an incident
A CI setting that stops all deploys while a flag is being changed
A flag that turns off one risky feature at runtime, without a deploy
A database trigger that disables writes when an error threshold is hit
questions.why: A kill switch is an operational flag around a risky dependency or feature, such as a new payment provider, so on-call can disable it in seconds without a deploy. It is scoped to one feature, not the whole system.
questions.asked: Shows you think about operating features, not just shipping them.

questions.q: Why must a feature flag that hides a new admin endpoint be checked on the server, not only in the React UI?
choices: Server-side checks are faster, because the flag is cached in memory
React cannot read feature flags without a full page reload
Hiding the button does not stop anyone calling the API directly
Flags checked in the browser are logged, which leaks the rollout
questions.why: A client-side flag only changes what is rendered; the endpoint stays reachable with any HTTP client. Anything that gates access or behaviour must be enforced by the API, with the UI flag as a convenience.
questions.asked: Links flags to the rule that the client is untrusted, which interviewers like to see applied.

questions.q: What does 'dark launching' a new backend feature mean?
choices: Deploying it outside business hours to reduce the number of affected users
Shipping it without release notes so users discover it gradually
Deploying it to production running on real traffic, with results hidden from users
Releasing it to one region first, while the other regions are kept offline until it is proven
questions.why: In a dark launch the new path runs in production, for example computing prices both ways or shadow-writing to a new store, while users still see the old result. It tests load and correctness on real traffic before anyone depends on it.
questions.asked: Shows familiarity with low-risk rollout techniques beyond on/off flags.

questions.q: You forked a repository. How do you bring your fork's `main` up to date with the original project?
choices: Run `git pull origin main`, which fetches from the original project automatically
Add the original as a remote such as `upstream`, fetch it, and merge or rebase
Delete the fork and fork it again whenever the original moves ahead of you
Push your `main` to the original, which merges its changes back into your fork
questions.why: `origin` is your fork; it knows nothing about new commits upstream. `git remote add upstream <url>`, `git fetch upstream` and then `git merge upstream/main` (or rebase) syncs it, and a push updates the fork on GitHub.
questions.asked: Everyday open-source workflow; shows you understand remotes are just named URLs.

questions.q: What does `git push -u origin feature/x` add over `git push origin feature/x`?
choices: It sets `origin/feature/x` as the upstream so plain `git push` and `git pull` work
It forces the push, overwriting any commits already on the remote branch
It pushes all local branches that have a matching name on the remote
It pushes the branch together with every tag that points into it, in a single operation
questions.why: `-u` (`--set-upstream`) records the tracking relationship, so later `git push`, `git pull` and `git status` ahead/behind counts know which remote branch to use. Setting `push.autoSetupRemote=true` does this automatically on first push.
questions.asked: Basic, but it explains the 'no upstream branch' error that confuses newcomers.

questions.q: Remote branches deleted on GitHub still show up in `git branch -r`. What removes the stale ones?
choices: `git branch -D origin/old-branch` for each one
`git gc --aggressive`
`git fetch --prune`
`git remote update --force`
questions.why: Remote-tracking branches are local copies that fetch updates but does not delete by default. `--prune` (or `fetch.prune=true`) removes those whose remote branch is gone. `git branch -D` targets local branches, not `origin/*` refs.
questions.asked: Small hygiene question that checks you know remote-tracking branches are local refs.

questions.q: How do you delete the branch `old-feature` from the remote?
choices: `git branch -d origin/old-feature`
`git push origin --delete old-feature`
`git remote remove old-feature`
`git fetch --prune --delete old-feature origin`
questions.why: Deleting a remote branch is a push of 'nothing' to that ref: `git push origin --delete old-feature` (or `git push origin :old-feature`). Deleting `origin/old-feature` locally only removes your tracking copy, and `git remote remove` deletes the whole remote configuration.
questions.asked: Everyday mechanics; the old colon syntax is a nice bonus to recognise.

questions.q: You set `git config --global pull.ff only`. What happens when your local branch and the remote have both moved on?
choices: Git merges them with a merge commit, as the default pull does
Git rebases your commits on top of the remote automatically
Git discards your local commits and fast-forwards to the remote
The pull refuses, so you choose to merge or rebase deliberately
questions.why: With `ff only`, pull succeeds only when your branch can simply move forward. If histories have diverged it stops, rather than creating a surprise merge commit. You then run `git pull --rebase` or `git merge` on purpose.
questions.asked: Shows you have an opinion about keeping history clean and know how to configure Git for it.

questions.q: What is the difference between `git merge --ff-only` and `git merge --no-ff`?
choices: `--ff-only` refuses unless it can fast-forward; `--no-ff` always creates a merge commit
`--ff-only` squashes the branch into one commit; `--no-ff` keeps all the branch's commits
`--ff-only` keeps your side on conflicts; `--no-ff` keeps theirs
`--ff-only` merges only the first commit; `--no-ff` merges the whole branch
questions.why: A fast-forward just moves the pointer when there is nothing to reconcile. `--ff-only` guarantees linear history or failure; `--no-ff` forces a merge commit even when a fast-forward was possible, which some teams want so each feature is one identifiable merge.
questions.asked: Tests whether you know what a fast-forward is, which underlies most merge-strategy discussions.

questions.q: You want a readable history of main showing one entry per merged PR, even though merge commits were used. Which option helps?
choices: `git log --merges-only --flat`
`git log --first-parent main`
`git log --no-walk main`
`git log --reverse main`
questions.why: Following only first parents walks main's own line: each merge commit appears, but the commits inside merged branches do not. `--merges` would list only merge commits, and `--no-walk` shows just the named commit. It is also the view `git bisect --first-parent` uses.
questions.asked: Useful on repos with merge commits; shows you can make history readable without rewriting it.

questions.q: You made two unrelated changes in one file and want to commit them separately. What do you use?
choices: `git commit --split file.ts`
`git add -p file.ts` to stage selected hunks
`git stash -p` and then two separate `git commit -a` runs
`git add file.ts` twice, once for each change
questions.why: Patch mode walks through each hunk and lets you stage only some, split hunks or edit them; commit, then stage the rest. Small, focused commits make review, revert and bisect far easier. There is no `--split` flag, and staging the file twice stages it all.
questions.asked: A signal of care about commit quality; interviewers like candidates who can shape commits deliberately.

questions.q: `git commit -am "wip"` did not include a new file you created. Why?
choices: `-a` only stages modified and deleted tracked files, never untracked ones
`-a` skips files larger than 1 MB unless `--all-sizes` is passed
The file is ignored, because new files are ignored until the first push
`-m` overrides `-a`, so only files that were already staged beforehand were committed
questions.why: `-a` is shorthand for staging changes to files Git already tracks. A new file must be added explicitly with `git add` the first time. This is a safety feature: stray build output does not sneak into commits.
questions.asked: A quick fundamentals check about what tracked means.

questions.q: What does `git diff --staged` show that plain `git diff` does not?
choices: Changes between your branch and the remote branch it tracks
Changes in the index that will go into the next commit
Changes to untracked files that have not been added yet
Changes stashed with `git stash` that have not been reapplied
questions.why: Plain `git diff` compares the working tree with the index (unstaged changes); `--staged` (alias `--cached`) compares the index with HEAD, which is exactly what `git commit` will record. Reviewing it before committing catches stray debug lines.
questions.asked: Tests the three-area model: working tree, index, HEAD.

questions.q: Your build left untracked files everywhere. What should you run before `git clean -fd` to avoid deleting something important?
choices: `git clean -n -d`, a dry run that lists what would be removed
`git stash`, which saves untracked files by default
`git status --ignored`, which marks files as safe to delete
`git reset --hard`, which moves untracked files into the system trash first
questions.why: `git clean` permanently deletes untracked files and nothing in Git can bring them back, so preview with `-n`. Plain `git stash` skips untracked files, and `reset --hard` does not touch them at all.
questions.asked: Tests caution with one of the few truly destructive Git commands.

questions.q: On macOS you rename `userCard.tsx` to `UserCard.tsx`. Git shows no change, and the Linux CI build fails with 'module not found'. What is going on?
choices: Git ignores file renames unless they also change the file's contents
Linux CI caches file names from its first build, so the runner cache needs to be cleared
The file system is case-insensitive, so Git never saw the rename; use `git mv`
TypeScript on Linux requires every file name to be lower case
questions.why: macOS and Windows file systems are usually case-insensitive, so Git (with `core.ignorecase`) does not notice a case-only rename, while imports now use the new case. `git mv userCard.tsx UserCard.tsx` records it. Linux is case-sensitive, so the old name in Git no longer matches.
questions.asked: A classic cross-platform bug; knowing the fix saves an hour of confusion.

questions.q: What does enabling `git config rerere.enabled true` give you?
choices: Git reapplies recorded conflict resolutions when the same conflict recurs
Git retries failed pushes automatically after the remote rejects them as non-fast-forward
Git re-runs pre-commit hooks after every rebase step
Git refuses to rebase any branch that has been pushed
questions.why: 'Reuse recorded resolution' remembers how you resolved a given conflict hunk and applies it automatically next time, which helps with repeated rebases of a long-lived branch. You still review and stage the result.
questions.asked: A niche but telling feature; people who rebase long branches often discover it the hard way.

questions.q: Why do teams use Git LFS for large binary assets such as design files or videos?
choices: LFS compresses binaries so they diff line by line like source code
LFS stores pointers in Git and the files elsewhere, keeping clones small
LFS encrypts binaries so they cannot be read from the repository
LFS lets Git merge binary files that conflict by keeping both versions side by side
questions.why: Every version of every binary committed normally lives in the history forever, so clones grow without bound. LFS commits small pointer files and downloads the real content on demand. It does not make binaries diffable, mergeable or encrypted.
questions.asked: Relevant when a repo gets slow; the strong answer knows history keeps every version.

questions.q: A repository uses a Git submodule for a shared library. After `git pull`, the library code is at the old version. Why?
choices: Submodules only update when the library's own `main` changes
Submodules are read-only, so they must be deleted and re-added to pick up a new version
The parent records a commit; run `git submodule update` to check it out
`git pull` updated it, but the editor is showing a cached copy
questions.why: The parent repository stores the exact commit of each submodule, and pulling updates that pointer but not the checked-out files. `git submodule update --init --recursive` (or `git pull --recurse-submodules`) syncs them. This pinning is also why submodules are awkward for fast-moving shared code.
questions.asked: Submodules confuse most people; the strong answer knows they pin a commit and weighs packages as an alternative.

questions.q: You need to view `config.json` exactly as it was in commit `a1b2c3d` without changing your working tree. Which command?
choices: `git checkout a1b2c3d config.json`
`git reset a1b2c3d config.json`
`git log -p a1b2c3d config.json`
`git show a1b2c3d:config.json`
questions.why: The `<rev>:<path>` syntax names a blob in that commit's tree and `git show` prints it. `checkout <rev> <path>` overwrites your working copy and index, and reset changes the index. `git log -p` shows diffs, not the whole file.
questions.asked: Handy during debugging; shows fluency with revision syntax.

questions.q: A teammate's commit on main introduced a bug and was later reverted. Now the fixed feature should land again. What is the cleanest way?
choices: Cherry-pick the original commit again, since reverts are ignored by Git
Revert the revert commit, then add the fix on top
Reset main to before the revert and force-push
Merge the original feature branch again, which reapplies it
questions.why: Git considers the original commits already in main, so re-merging the old branch brings nothing back. Reverting the revert restores the change in the open, and the follow-up commit fixes the bug. Force-pushing shared main is never the answer.
questions.asked: Tests understanding that a revert is a new commit, not an erasure.

questions.q: What does `git cherry-pick -x <sha>` add over a plain cherry-pick?
choices: It excludes merge commits from the pick
It deletes the original commit after copying it
It notes the source commit's SHA in the new commit message
It picks the commit without running any of the local commit hooks
questions.why: `-x` appends '(cherry picked from commit ...)' to the message, which is useful when backporting a fix to a release branch because it links the two commits for anyone reading history later. The original commit is untouched.
questions.asked: Backporting hygiene; relevant to release-branch workflows.

questions.q: Your monorepo clone takes 20 minutes. Which clone option downloads full history but fetches file contents only when needed?
choices: `git clone --depth 1`
`git clone --single-branch --no-tags`
`git clone --filter=blob:none`
`git clone --bare`
questions.why: A blobless partial clone downloads all commits and trees but fetches blobs lazily, so log and blame still work. `--depth 1` truncates history, which breaks describe and blame, and `--bare` has no working tree at all.
questions.asked: Relevant for large repos and CI; knowing the trade-off with shallow clones is the point.

questions.q: You want to use your work email in one folder of repositories and your personal email everywhere else. What does Git offer?
choices: A `.gitemail` file committed at the root of each repository
Setting `user.email` in `.gitignore`
An environment variable that must be exported in every terminal session
A conditional include such as `includeIf "gitdir:~/work/"`
questions.why: `includeIf` in the global config loads another config file for repositories under a path, so work repos pick up the work email automatically. A per-repo `git config user.email` also works but is easy to forget.
questions.asked: A practical setup question; it prevents personal addresses leaking into company history.

questions.q: What does a signed commit or tag (GPG, SSH or Sigstore signature) prove?
choices: That the commit passed CI before it was pushed
That the holder of a specific key created it
That the code was reviewed by another developer
That the author email address is verified by GitHub
questions.why: Anyone can set `user.name` and `user.email` to anything, so author fields prove nothing. A signature proves possession of a private key, which the hosting service can map to an account. It says nothing about review or CI.
questions.asked: Asked where supply-chain integrity matters; the strong answer knows author fields are unauthenticated.

questions.q: What is the difference between ESLint and Prettier in a JS/TS project?
choices: ESLint formats code; Prettier finds bugs such as unused variables
ESLint only works on JavaScript; Prettier only works on TypeScript
ESLint runs only in CI pipelines; Prettier runs only inside the developer's editor
ESLint finds problems and bad patterns; Prettier only rewrites formatting
questions.why: Prettier is an opinionated formatter with almost no rules about correctness; ESLint analyses code for bugs and conventions such as unused variables or missing hook dependencies. Teams turn off ESLint's stylistic rules so the two never fight.
questions.asked: A quick tooling-literacy check.

questions.q: CI runs `eslint . --max-warnings 0`. What does that achieve?
choices: Warnings are suppressed so only errors are printed
Any warning fails the build, so warnings cannot pile up
ESLint stops after the first file with a warning
Warnings are converted into autofixes and committed back to the branch
questions.why: Without it, warnings never fail the build and accumulate until nobody reads them. With a zero budget, a warning must be fixed or explicitly disabled with a reason. Autofix is `--fix` and needs a separate commit step.
questions.asked: Tests whether you think about lint signal decaying over time.

questions.q: Why do repositories include an `.editorconfig` file?
choices: It configures the linter's rules for every language in the repo
It stops the editor from opening files outside the repository
It sets indentation, line endings and final newlines across editors
It stores the list of recommended editor extensions and themes for the project
questions.why: EditorConfig is read by most editors to apply basic whitespace settings per file type, so a teammate on a different editor does not reindent files. Recommended extensions live in editor-specific files such as `.vscode/extensions.json`.
questions.asked: Small but practical team hygiene.

questions.q: Which statement about `npx some-cli` is correct?
choices: It installs the package globally so later runs of the same command are instant
It runs the local binary if installed, else fetches the package to run
It only runs packages already listed in `package.json`
It runs the command with elevated permissions
questions.why: `npx` resolves binaries from `node_modules/.bin` first and otherwise downloads the package to a cache and runs it, prompting first in recent npm versions. Relying on the local devDependency keeps everyone on the version in the lockfile.
questions.asked: Helps explain why tools should be devDependencies rather than global installs.

questions.q: Your team keeps a `CHANGELOG.md`. What makes it genuinely useful to users?
choices: Grouping entries by version with added, changed, fixed and breaking notes
Pasting the full output of `git log` for each release
Listing every commit author and the number of lines they changed in each release
Keeping it in a wiki, separate from the code it describes
questions.why: Users need to know what changed and whether they must act, which means human-readable entries per version with breaking changes called out. Raw commit logs include refactors and typos and hide what matters.
questions.asked: Shows you think about the people consuming a release, not just producing it.

questions.q: What is the difference between continuous delivery and continuous deployment?
choices: Delivery deploys every commit to production automatically; deployment batches releases weekly
Delivery keeps every build releasable; deployment actually ships each one automatically
Delivery is for frontends; deployment is for backend services
Delivery needs manual tests; deployment has no tests
questions.why: Continuous delivery means any green build could go to production at the push of a button; continuous deployment removes the button so every green commit ships. Both need automated tests and a reliable pipeline.
questions.asked: Vocabulary question often asked to check you are not using the terms interchangeably.

questions.q: A deploy script runs `kubectl apply` then immediately reports success. A minute later the new pods are crash-looping. What was missing?
choices: Waiting for the rollout to complete, for example `kubectl rollout status`
Running `kubectl apply` twice so the change is definitely registered
A `sleep 60` after apply to give the cluster time to settle
Deleting the old pods by hand before applying the new manifest so none linger
questions.why: `apply` only submits the desired state; the rollout happens afterwards. `kubectl rollout status` (or the platform's equivalent) blocks until new pods are ready or the rollout fails, so the pipeline can report failure and roll back. A fixed sleep is guesswork.
questions.asked: Tests whether your pipeline verifies the deploy rather than just firing it.

questions.q: Why do mature pipelines run a smoke test against production right after each deploy?
choices: To warm the CDN cache before users arrive
To confirm the running release can serve a real request end to end
To replace the unit tests, which cannot run in CI
To load-test production at peak capacity after every deploy, before users arrive
questions.why: A healthy process is not a working app: a smoke test hits a key endpoint or page and fails the deploy, triggering a rollback, if configuration, secrets or connectivity are wrong. It is a few requests, not a load test.
questions.asked: Connects to 'green pipeline, broken production'; the strong answer ties it to automatic rollback.

questions.q: What is an expand/contract (parallel change) migration?
choices: Scaling the database up for a migration, then back down afterwards
Adding the new schema alongside the old, moving code over, then removing the old
Running the migration on a read replica first, then promoting that replica to primary
Compressing a table before a migration so it finishes faster
questions.why: To rename a column safely you add the new one, write both and backfill, switch reads, and only drop the old column in a later release. Every intermediate state works with both the old and new code, which is what rolling deploys and rollbacks need.
questions.asked: Asked for zero-downtime deploy discussions; naming the steps is the strong answer.

questions.q: In GitHub Actions, what is a job-level `if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'` on the deploy job for?
choices: It makes the job run first, before any other job in the workflow
It lets the job read secrets that are otherwise hidden from branches
It makes the deploy job run only for pushes to main
It rebases the branch onto main before the job starts
questions.why: The condition is evaluated before the job starts; on PRs and other branches the deploy job is skipped while build and test still run. Combining it with an environment protection rule gives a second guard for production.
questions.asked: Everyday pipeline authoring; shows you keep deploys off feature branches.

questions.q: Your GitHub Actions minutes bill doubled. Which change usually saves the most without losing signal?
choices: Running the full suite only once a night instead of on every PR
Cancelling superseded runs, caching dependencies and adding job timeouts
Moving every job onto the largest runner size so each run finishes sooner
Removing the lint and type-check steps, which rarely fail
questions.why: Superseded runs on busy PRs, cold dependency installs and hung jobs are the usual waste. Nightly-only testing delays feedback, and removing cheap checks saves little while losing the fastest signals.
questions.asked: Tests cost awareness and knowledge of the cheap wins.

questions.q: What does `git maintenance start` (or the automatic `git gc`) do for a large local repository?
choices: Deletes local branches that were merged more than 30 days ago
Repacks objects and updates the commit graph in the background
Pushes unpushed commits to a backup remote on a schedule
Rewrites history to strip out any files larger than 100 MB from old commits
questions.why: Maintenance tasks pack loose objects, prefetch from remotes and write the commit-graph file so log, status and fetch stay fast. They never delete branches or rewrite history; only unreachable objects past their expiry are pruned.
questions.asked: A niche question that shows curiosity about why Git stays fast.

questions.q: You accidentally ran `git stash drop` on a stash you needed. Is it recoverable?
choices: No, dropping a stash deletes its commit objects immediately
Yes, but only with `git stash undo` within five minutes
Yes, via `git reflog stash`, which keeps a record of every dropped stash entry
Usually, since `git fsck --unreachable` can find the dangling stash commit
questions.why: A stash is stored as commits; dropping removes the ref but the objects remain until garbage collection. `git fsck --unreachable | grep commit` (or the SHA printed when you dropped it) lets you `git stash apply <sha>`. There is no `stash undo`, and the stash reflog loses the dropped entry.
questions.asked: Deep recovery knowledge; interviewers use it to see if you understand stashes are commits.

questions.q: What does `git switch -` do?
choices: Switches to the branch you had checked out before the current one
Creates a new branch named after the current commit's SHA
Detaches HEAD at the current commit so you can experiment
Switches to the default branch configured for the remote
questions.why: Like `cd -` in a shell, `-` means the previously checked-out branch (`@{-1}`), so you can bounce between a feature branch and main quickly. It does not create or detach anything.
questions.asked: A small fluency signal; people who use Git all day know the shortcuts.
